title: Interest Rate Caps, Competition, and Strategic Borrowing: Evidence from Kenya
affiliations: , Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Interest Rate Caps, Competition, and Strategic Borrowing: Evidence from Kenya
detail.abstract:
We study Kenya’s 2016 interest-rate regulation, which capped bank lending rates but left one digital platform, called M-Shwari, exempt on the lending side while imposing a deposit-rate floor across all lenders in the market. Using borrower-level administrative data, survey data, and an RD around the implementation date, we show three main results. First, lending on the exempt platform rose, but with the safest borrowers substituting away toward cheaper capped credit. Second, riskier borrowers increase their savings to build up their credit limits. Third, on the supply side, M-Shwari raises the limits for the safest borrowers in an attempt to retain them. We build and estimate a simple model of screening and credit limit-setting to interpret these reallocations and compute welfare. The observed carve-out for M-Shwari preserves access for high-risk borrowers but yields a slight aggregate welfare decline relative to pre-policy. However, a uniform (across all lenders) interest rate cap counterfactual generates substantially larger welfare losses by entirely eliminating credit for high-risk borrowers.

title: When Desire Outruns Reality: The Habenular Algorithm Beneath the History of Philosophy
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: When Desire Outruns Reality: The Habenular Algorithm Beneath the History of Philosophy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Self
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self

detail.abstract: Twenty-five centuries of philosophy, East and West, can be read as a sustained and largely unconscious project of managing a single biological event: the organismic response to the gap between desire and reality. Donald Nathanson's formulation-when desire outruns reality, shame ensues-provides the affective language for what the lateral habenula, a phylogenetically ancient structure in the epithalamic region of the diencephalon, implements neurophysiologically as negative prediction error. This position paper maps the major philosophical traditions onto that substrate, identifies three fundamental strategies-reduce desire, improve reality, reframe the gap-and argues that Silvan Tomkins' affect theory and the ethical teaching of the Beatitudes arrive, by different routes, closest to the biological bedrock. The paper concludes with Tomkins' concept of nuclear scripts, which explains not merely why we suffer but why insight so rarely resolves that suffering. Philosophy has not ended. It has, at last, located its foundation.

title: On the Negative Consequences of Low-Wage Offshoring for Innovation
affiliations: Statistics Canada, York University and University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: On the Negative Consequences of Low-Wage Offshoring for Innovation
detail.abstract:
Conventional wisdom holds that offshoring intermediates to China stimulates innovation. This is not entirely compelling. On the one hand, (a) offshoring lowers marginal costs and expands sales, thereby increasing the returns to innovation, especially for large firms. On the other hand, (b) offshoring low-quality intermediates reduces the costs of older-generation products, thereby reducing the returns to innovating into newer generations. We examine these two opposing forces over 2002-2011 for 6,024 Canadian firms. Our empirical strategy regresses measures of innovation, such as R&D, on imports of intermediate inputs. To address endogeneity, we construct a model-consistent shift-share instrument whose shocks are the often-dramatic improvements in the quality of HS6 Chinese intermediate inputs. We find that greater offshoring reduced R&D spending over 2002-2011 by 15% as (1) firms engaged in R&D in 2002 reduced their expenditures, and (2) firms not initially engaged in R&D were discouraged from starting up new R&D projects. Our model explains these findings: Rising quality of Chinese intermediates is a positive supply shock (rather than a negative China shock) that raises profits for all offshorers, raises innovation for the largest offshorers (channel a above), and lowers innovation for all other offshorers (channel b). These predictions are confirmed in the data.

title: The Postpandemic U.S. Immigration Surge: New Facts and Inflationary Implications
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, , Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas

detail.title: The Postpandemic U.S. Immigration Surge: New Facts and Inflationary Implications
detail.abstract:
The U.S. experienced an extraordinary surge in immigration from 2021 to 2024, which triggered widespread discussions about its macroeconomic impact, particularly on inflation. To determine the impact of the immigration surge, we first document the salient features of these new immigrants: they are primarily low-skilled relative to the existing workforce and more likely to be hand-to-mouth consumers. We then incorporate these features into a heterogeneous agent model with capital-skill complementarity. We find that the supply- and demand-side effects of the immigration surge roughly cancel out, causing a negligible response of inflation.

title: Competitive Exposure and Entrepreneurial Experimentation
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Competitive Exposure and Entrepreneurial Experimentation
detail.abstract:
Entrepreneurs learn by experimenting, but experiment choices are often public. A closed beta, private pilot, or public launch not only generates evidence; it also reveals what kind of entrepreneur would choose that action. We develop a dynamic model in which a founder chooses between stealthy and public experiments while potential entrants infer from both actions and outcomes. Public outcomes are modelled as garblings of the founder's private experimental evidence, so public leakage informs outsiders without giving the founder information beyond the private signal already observed. The key state variable is competitive exposure: the public runway before entry becomes attractive. Exposure is depleted by two forces, leakage burn from public outcomes, and action burn from public inference about experiment choice. This distinction implies that competition can distort experiment design without forcing earlier scale: lower-confidence founders choose stealthier tests, while higher-confidence founders spend exposure to obtain faster private learning through more public tests. Scale is accelerated only when exposure reduces the value of waiting more than it reduces the value of scaling. Finally, exogenous funding gates make observable scale more selective and, therefore, more informative to entrants. The analysis shows that entrepreneurial experimentation is not merely private learning under uncertainty; it is public action under competitive inference.

title: Opt In? Opt Out?
affiliations: Harvard University, Boston University and Harvard University - Business School (HBS)

detail.title: Opt In? Opt Out?
detail.abstract:
Cadaveric organ shortages leave thousands without life-saving transplants each year. Countries differ in using opt-in (informed consent) or opt-out (presumed consent) systems for donor registration. Using newly assembled cross-country panel data and an event-study design, this paper provides evidence that presumed-consent laws increase organ donation only when strictly enforced and family veto power is limited; weak opt-out regimes show negligible or even negative effects. A theoretical signaling model provides a plausible mechanism when opt-in or opt-out yields more donations, emphasizing the roles of donation propensity, signaling costs, and the family’s ability to overturn defaults. A large laboratory experiment further tests these mechanisms, showing that opt-in generally produces equal or higher donation rates unless signaling is costly and family veto power is minimal. The results underscore that defaults alone rarely increase donations unless paired with strong institutional enforcement.

title: Extreme Equilibria: The Benefits of Correlation
affiliations: Analysis Group, Princeton University and Princeton University

detail.title: Extreme Equilibria: The Benefits of Correlation
detail.abstract:
Correlated equilibria arise naturally when agents communicate or rely on intermediaries such as recommendation systems. We study when a given Nash equilibrium can be improved within the set of correlated equilibria for general objectives. Our key insight is a detail-free criterion: any Nash equilibrium with three or more randomizing agents is generically improvable. We refine this insight to specific classes of games and objectives, including Pareto and utilitarian welfare, and provide constructive methods to obtain improvements. Our findings underscore the ubiquity of improvable Nash equilibria and the crucial role of correlation in enhancing strategic outcomes.

title: The Causal Effects of Expected Depreciations
affiliations: Inter-American Development Bank, University of California, San Diego (UCSD), Universidad de los Andes and Inter-American Development Bank

detail.title: The Causal Effects of Expected Depreciations
detail.abstract:
We construct a novel measure of one-year-ahead exchange rate forecasts and nowcasts for non-financial firms. We then study a randomized information intervention that provides a subset of firms with a publicly available exchange rate forecast. This information treatment persistently shifts exchange rate expectations and perceptions, with stronger effects for non-exporting firms. We link survey responses with administrative customs data and estimate a positive intertemporal elasticity of import demand to exogenous changes in expected future exchange rates. Our findings highlight the role of intertemporal substitution after anticipated changes in trade costs.

title: Authority Figures and the Polarization of Gender Norms
affiliations: American University of Beirut, Boston University - Department of Economics, Simon Fraser University (SFU), World Bank - Development Impact and Simon Fraser University (SFU)

detail.title: Authority Figures and the Polarization of Gender Norms
detail.abstract:
This paper examines how authority figures in higher education shape gender norms over the long run. We exploit the random assignment of first-year students to faculty advisors at an elite university in the Middle East and combine administrative records with an alumni survey measuring gender attitudes up to 24 years later. Women assigned to female advisors adopt more egalitarian views about politics and work, while men become more conservative. These effects are strongest among religious students and in male-dominated STEM fields, where female authority is especially counter-stereotypical. The effects may persist through reinforcement, as women assigned to female advisors later sort toward female instructors and more gender-themed courses. Our results do not appear to be driven by generic exposure to successful women. Instead, they point to a distinct role for authority in transmitting gender norms: randomized exposure to high-achieving female peers has little effect, while the largest impacts come from senior and high-value-added female advisors. A simple framework combining belief updating and identity-based status threat helps explain these patterns of female empowerment and male backlash. More broadly, our findings reveal a progress paradox whereby gains in female representation in elite authority expand opportunities for women while intensifying backlash among men, thereby deepening gender polarization.

title: How does Medicare Eligibility affect Choice and Utilization? Evidence from Veterans
affiliations: University of California, Irvine, Department of Veterans Affairs and Stanford University - VA Palo Alto Health Care System

detail.title: How does Medicare Eligibility affect Choice and Utilization? Evidence from Veterans
detail.abstract:
We examine how Medicare affects health care utilization for those who age in with a more narrow health insurance network by studying veterans enrolled in the Veterans Health Administration (VA). Given the limited geographic density of VA hospitals, we posit that Medicare expands the insurance network for VA enrollees. Using regression discontinuity methods, we find that veterans' inpatient hospitalization rate increases by approximately 3.3 percent at 65. Further, there are large reallocations across health insurance payers. Individuals increasingly use Medicare for hospitalizations once it becomes available, while VA, commercial, and other federal insurance programs are used less. We also find substantial reallocations among individuals that gain access to hospitals closer to their homes and among those who visit the hospital for more postponeable medical procedures. However, we do not find evidence that the average quality rating of the hospital selected at 65 changes nor do we find evidence that VA hospital wait times affect the move to Medicare; rather, individuals choose hospitals that are relatively closer. Lastly, our results suggest that Medicare may compete with other federal programs to provide health care for select populations, such as veterans.

title: Secondary Markets for VC-Backed Startup Equity
affiliations: Owen Graduate School of Management at Vanderbilt University,  and Vanderbilt University - Finance

detail.title: Secondary Markets for VC-Backed Startup Equity
detail.abstract: This paper provides the first systematic evidence on secondary markets for equity in VC-backed startups, a fast-growing segment of private capital markets. Using proprietary data from a large intermediary, we show that shares typically trade at a discount to prior venture capital valuations, with discounts narrowing when buyer demand is strong. We find that market activity responds to new information: in an event study, order flow and prices react quickly to VC financing events. Furthermore, secondary prices are forward-looking and predict future VC valuations. These signals are partially incorporated by mutual funds valuing their startup holdings. By providing both liquidity and price discovery, secondary markets are becoming an integral part of private capital markets, and their importance is likely to grow as startups remain private longer.

title: Separations Revisited: Do Layoffs or Quits Drive Lower Separation Rates in High-Quality Firms?
affiliations: Georgetown University, CEMFI and Centre for Monetary and Financial Studies (CEMFI)

detail.title: Separations Revisited: Do Layoffs or Quits Drive Lower Separation Rates in High-Quality Firms?
detail.abstract:
A well-known empirical regularity is that high-productivity firms have lower worker separation rates, but it is unclear whether this pattern reflects quits or layoffs. Using matched employer-employee data from Brazil that distinguish the reason for each separation, we show that the productivity-separation gradient is driven primarily by layoffs rather than quits. We then propose and test a mechanism in which downward wage rigidity prevents firms from adjusting wages in response to adverse shocks, causing those shocks to translate into layoffs. High-productivity firms are less exposed because their larger markdowns provide a buffer between productivity and wages. Consistent with this mechanism, we find that firms with higher markdowns have lower layoff rates, and that markets with stronger wage rigidity exhibit both higher layoff rates and a steeper productivity-layoff gradient. These findings suggest that productivity differences across firms shape not only wages, but also workers' exposure to job loss.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Property Governance: Challenges for Public Administration Meenaz,independent researcher, May,2026
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Property Governance: Challenges for Public Administration Meenaz,independent researcher, May,2026

declarations.funderStatement: Self funded

detail.abstract: This study examines the intersection of artificial intelligence, intellectual property, and public administration and exploring how AI helps reshaping innovation processes and regulatory frameworks. Through a mixed-method approach, combining a systematic literature review and expert insights, the research explores AI's disruptive impact on IP regimes and administrative governance. The findings reveal a gap between traditional IP laws and the rapid pace of AI innovation, highlighting the urgent need for public institutions to develop flexible and adaptive governance models. Based on the previous insights, this paper offers concrete policy recommendations to ensure AI's integration into IP governance is ethical, accountable, transparent, and aligned with public interests.

title: Earnings Management and Price Informativeness
affiliations: Stanford University,  and Princeton University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Earnings Management and Price Informativeness
detail.abstract:
We investigate the relationship between stock prices and future earnings in China's A-share market. In the cross-section, firms with higher market valuations report higher earnings over the subsequent one to five years, suggesting that stock prices contain information about future fundamentals. In the time series, however, we find evidence of earnings reversal: higher stock prices predict weaker earnings growth three to five years ahead, consistent with short-term earnings management induced by stock-price pressures. We further document such earnings management through non-recurring gains and losses (NRGLs) and use the 2020 delisting rule reform as a natural experiment to examine these mechanisms.

title: Bachelors Without Bachelor's: Gender Gaps in Education and Declining Marriage Rates
affiliations: Yale University, Cornell University and Harvard University

detail.title: Bachelors Without Bachelor's: Gender Gaps in Education and Declining Marriage Rates
detail.abstract:
Over the past half-century, U.S. four-year colleges have shifted from enrolling mostly men to enrolling mostly women, while the economic position of non-college men has weakened markedly. We examine how these changes correspond with the evolving structure of marriage markets across cohorts and places. As college men have become increasingly scarce, college women have maintained stable marriage rates by marrying high-earning non-college men. This shift—combined with the broader economic decline of non-college men—has sharply reduced the pool of economically stable partners available to non-college women: the share of non-college men who earn above the national median and are not married to college women has fallen by more than 50%. Cross-area evidence shows that education gaps in marriage are smaller where non-college men face lower rates of joblessness and incarceration. Taken together, the evidence suggests that deteriorating outcomes for men have primarily undermined the marriage prospects of non-college women.

title: The Persistence of Power: How Family Origins Shape Political Representation and Policy
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin, University of Texas at Austin, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia

detail.title: The Persistence of Power: How Family Origins Shape Political Representation and Policy
detail.abstract:
In the United States, long hailed as the land of opportunity, is access to political office truly open across society, or do the most privileged children disproportionately rise to enter political life? This question speaks to a longstanding concern that elite families may entrench themselves in positions of power, reproducing a form of hereditary privilege within a democratic system. We study the family backgrounds of U.S. politicians over the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and show that children from wealthy and privileged households have been substantially overrepresented in elected office. This imbalance has changed little over time and, at the highest levels of office, varies little across political parties. To test whether political access depends on family resources, we exploit the sudden economic shock caused by the end of slavery. Despite the large and concentrated losses at the top of the wealth distribution, the children of slaveholders continued to enter government at high rates. Finally, we examine whether politicians' socioeconomic origins shape policy by constructing a new sample of close elections linked to detailed information on U.S. House candidates' family backgrounds. Comparing otherwise similar districts in which a candidate from a high socioeconomic status family narrowly wins rather than loses, we find that districts represented by higher status candidates are less likely to support pro-tax positions in roll-call voting. Together, the evidence across our analyses shows that family background strongly predicts entry into political office and has measurable consequences for policy choices.

title: Youth Mental Health and School Smartphone Bans: Early Evidence
affiliations: National Bureau of Economic Research

detail.title: Youth Mental Health and School Smartphone Bans: Early Evidence
detail.abstract:
This paper is the first to examine the causal effects of school smartphone bans on the mental health of youth in the US. Time series data show that the mental health of youth has been declining for the past decade. Several researchers argue that easy access to social media and other internet sites provided by smartphones is to blame. To provide causal evidence of the effects of these bans, I rely on synthetic difference-in-difference models and the National Survey of Children’s Health (NSCH) from 2016 to 2024. Currently, there are data for only one state with two post-ban periods and two states with one post-ban period, which makes the results preliminary evidence only. The outcome variables are screentime and measures of psychological wellbeing. Overall, these early results provide no clear evidence that the school ban policy reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing. Future studies with additional years of data, when they are available, are needed to increase power and to estimate the longer-term effects of school bans on youth mental health.

title: How Much of Mortgage Default Reflects Life Events? Evidence on Causal Attribution under Probabilistic Behavior
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and University of California Berkeley

detail.title: How Much of Mortgage Default Reflects Life Events? Evidence on Causal Attribution under Probabilistic Behavior
detail.abstract: We develop a latent structural propensity model of mortgage default that separates incentives from execution and characterizes causal attribution when default behavior is probabilistic. In this setting, observed outcomes no longer reveal their underlying cause, and attribution depends on behavioral responses and the informativeness of comparison groups. We show that commonly used benchmark-based attribution methods need not recover the underlying causal share and can overstate the role of life events. Because the benchmark-based estimator is nonlinear in observable moments, aggregation across heterogeneous environments introduces additional distortion, so causal shares are not identified from benchmark comparisons alone.

title: Four Mechanisms of Convergent Phenomena
affiliations: , Chiang Mai University and Webster University in Tashkent

detail.title: Four Mechanisms of Convergent Phenomena

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No
declarations.ethicsApproval: No consent needed
declarations.funderStatement: Self Funded

publicationDetails.detailsText: no.. it is a continue of previous paper

detail.abstract:
Part I of The Aden Effect (van Rooyen, Nandhakwang and Ganeshu, 2026b) established that contemporary global phenomena exhibit convergent integration across economic, political, technological, and military domains, and that the established disciplines cannot account for what they are observing because their analytical instruments treat the integrating variables as exogenous to one another. The diagnostic work of Part I, building on the framework originally proposed in van Rooyen, Nandhakwang and Ganeshu (2026a), demonstrated that something is happening the disciplines cannot describe. It did not, however, establish what that something was. The present paper takes the next analytical step. It argues that the integrative property identified in the diagnostic work is not a feature added to otherwise stable systems but a set of operating mechanisms through which the systems themselves are constituted, and it identifies four such mechanisms: feedback loops that compound across cognitive, geopolitical, energy-climate, institutional-formation, and material-substrate domains; the structural collapse of accountability under conditions of AI-human hybrid decision-making; a cognitive transformation that has displaced the substrate on which institutions and analytical disciplines depend; and the emergence of parallel civilizations operating on incompatible regulatory, financial, and political architectures. The four mechanisms are presented sequentially for analytical clarity but are argued to be expressions of the same integration operating through different channels.

The paper’s contribution is methodological as well as substantive. It proposes that the unit of analysis appropriate to the current period is the mechanism rather than the discrete phenomenon, with disciplinary tools deployed as instruments for clarifying specific aspects of mechanisms in operation rather than as comprehensive frameworks. The cases the paper develops are drawn from events occurring in real time as the paper is being written including the Nvidia export-control cycle, the Anthropic–Department of Defense litigation, Operation Economic Fury and the Tether–Nobitex contrast, the Musk–European Union regulatory confrontation, and the late-April 2026 rupture in transatlantic alliance relationships, with each case selected because it illustrates the relevant mechanism operating across what the disciplines treat as separate domains. The paper concludes that the analytical work the disciplines have refused to do must now be undertaken by analysts willing to operate at the mechanism level, with the understanding that the mechanisms themselves continue to evolve as the integration deepens. A companion paper (van Rooyen, Nandhakwang and Ganeshu, 2026c) translates the framework into operational practice for analysts working under these conditions.

title: Agentic AI and Human-in-the-Loop Interventions: Field Experimental Evidence from Alibaba's Customer Service Operations
affiliations: Zhejiang University - International Business School, School of Management, Fudan University, Fudan University - School of Management, Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business and Alibaba Group

detail.title: Agentic AI and Human-in-the-Loop Interventions: Field Experimental Evidence from Alibaba's Customer Service Operations
detail.abstract: Agentic AI systems that autonomously perform service tasks are being rapidly deployed in customer service operations. However, limited evidence exists regarding how human-in-the-loop interventions influence service outcomes when agentic AI failures result in both cognitive and emotional consequences. We investigate this issue through a randomized field experiment conducted on the Taobao platform of Alibaba. Workers in the treatment condition supervised an agentic AI system that resolved AI-eligible chats while continuing to handle AI-ineligible chats. In contrast, workers in the control condition resolved all chats without agentic AI. The findings indicate that the deployment of agentic AI reduces the average duration of chats and has limited effects on retrial rates, but substantially decreases customer ratings for AI-eligible chats. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the effectiveness of human intervention on AI-eligible chats depends on the nature of AI failure, the postescalation human intervention effort, and the timing of intervention. Human intervention preserves service quality in algorithm-triggered technical escalations, i.e., unresolved customer issues beyond the AI's capability, but is less effective in algorithm-triggered emotional escalations, i.e., cases where customers have expressed frustration or dissatisfaction. These differences are partially explained by variations in the post-escalation intervention effort of human workers across different escalation types. For emotional escalations triggered by algorithms, workers exhibited lower engagement-they sent fewer messages, contributed to a smaller share of total chat rounds, and demonstrated less proactivity in information seeking and solution provision. We further find that early intervention is essential for sustaining high post-escalation intervention effort. Finally, we document a positive spillover effect on AI-ineligible chats, as treated workers adapted their multitasking workflow to devote greater attention to these chats. These findings offer implications for human-in-the-loop process design in human-AI collaboration systems.

title: UNIVERSITY OF LUCKNOW ASSIGNMENT ON CUSTOM CLEARANCE OF IMPORTS
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: UNIVERSITY OF LUCKNOW ASSIGNMENT ON CUSTOM CLEARANCE OF IMPORTS
detail.abstract:
This assignment explains the concept and procedure of custom clearance of imports in international trade. Custom clearance is an important legal process through which imported goods are examined, verified, and approved by customs authorities before entering the domestic market. The study highlights the meaning, importance, and objectives of import customs clearance and discusses the role of customs authorities, importers, and customs brokers in ensuring smooth trade operations.
The assignment also explains the step-by-step procedure of import customs clearance, including filing of the bill of entry, submission of required documents, duty assessment, inspection of goods, and final release of consignments. Important documents such as commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading, insurance certificate, and certificate of origin are discussed in detail.
In addition, the study focuses on common problems faced during import clearance, such as incorrect documentation, delays, tariff classification issues, and customs disputes. Suggestions for improving the efficiency of customs clearance through proper documentation, digital systems, and awareness of import regulations are also included.
Overall, the assignment emphasizes that efficient customs clearance is essential for lawful international trade, timely delivery of goods, revenue collection, and reduction of business risks in import operations.

title: Evolutionary Alpha Miner: Family-Aware Symbolic Alpha Discovery with LLM-Guided Hybridization A Feedback-Driven Framework for Correlation-Aware Formulaic Alpha Search

detail.title: Evolutionary Alpha Miner: Family-Aware Symbolic Alpha Discovery with LLM-Guided Hybridization A Feedback-Driven Framework for Correlation-Aware Formulaic Alpha Search

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, human data, animals, or clinical intervention. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes Evolutionary Alpha Miner, a family-aware evolutionary framework for formulaic alpha discovery. The framework represents alpha expressions as symbolic programs, groups nearduplicate expressions into normalized seed families, and uses ordered A-B parent pairs to generate new candidates. In each pair, the A parent acts as the primary signal backbone, while the B parent is restricted to a weak role such as a gate, regime condition, data-domain modifier, or correlation breaker. Large language models are used as constrained symbolic program synthesizers rather than as unconstrained formula generators. The framework is designed as a closed-loop research system. It records parent-family usage, tag-pair outcomes, mutation modes, simulation results, audit labels, and failure reasons. These records form a feedback memory that guides later exploration and repair. This design separates two tasks that are often mixed together in alpha research: broad candidate exploration and targeted failure-aware refinement. Across 45 search rounds, the system selected 4,620 parent pairs and generated 3,857 valid symbolic candidates. Of these, 3,214 obtained simulation identifiers, corresponding to an executable-candidate rate of 83.33%. The process produced 65 confirmed candidates and 862 strong-but-not-landed candidates. The latter group consists of candidates with promising signal characteristics that fail one or more final constraints, and therefore serves as a structured repair pool. Empirical summaries show that heterogeneous tag pairs such as fundamental+volume, volume+price, and option+price are associated with different success profiles. Mutation modes such as mild correlation breaking, regime hybridization, and weak gating also exhibit distinct outcome patterns. The results suggest that family-aware symbolic hybridization can produce a diverse and diagnostically useful candidate population for formulaic alpha research. The paper does not claim to identify deployable trading strategies, nor does it disclose private alpha expressions, proprietary data, credentials, or confidential implementation details. Its contribution is methodological: it presents a structured, feedbackdriven approach to correlation-aware symbolic candidate generation.

title: Orchestrating Business, Technology and People Capabilities for Digital Transformation and Operational Performance in Oil and Gas EPC Organizations Purpose

detail.title: Orchestrating Business, Technology and People Capabilities for Digital Transformation and Operational Performance in Oil and Gas EPC Organizations Purpose

keywords: Oil and gas EPC industry organizations

detail.abstract: This study examines how business, technology, and people capabilities jointly contribute to the development of digital transformation and subsequently enhance operational performance in oil and gas engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) organizations. This study provides empirical evidence on the role of integrated organizational capabilities in enabling effective digital transformation in complex project-based environments. Originality/Value This study contributes to the digital transformation and strategic management literature by empirically validating a capability-based framework within the underexplored context of oil and gas energy project organizations. Unlike prior studies that primarily focus on individual capability dimensions or stable organizational settings, this research highlights the combined effect of business, technology, and people capabilities in project-based environments characterized by high complexity and coordination requirements. This study provides practical insights for managers seeking to enhance operational performance through integrated digital transformation initiatives.

title: Smart Mobility in the MENA Region
affiliations: World Economic Forum

detail.title: Smart Mobility in the MENA Region

contentType.other: MENA Tech 2024: Mapping the Technology Landscape, Brown Lloyd James BLJ Worldwide, World Economic Forum- Global Agenda on the Future of Economic Progress and Artificial Intelligence

detail.abstract: This research uses mapped urbanization, PESTEL analysis, Smart City projects, and socioeconomic impacts to analyze the MENA region's outlook on smart mobility. Countries in the MENA region are implementing large-scale smart mobility projects to combat modern urbanization challenges such as traffic congestion, informality, and pollution. Smart mobility in MENA has the potential to solve many of the urbanization challenges facing the region as well as enhance the quality of life of its growing population. Yet the two critical factors of (a) political stability and (b) adequate financial resources are strong necessary conditions for positive longterm impact. With a forward-looking young population and vivid demographics of modern cultural development, many of the MENA countries are expected to pioneer in smart mobility systems in usage and longer-term co-production. Affordability, accessibility, and efficiently usable are important conditions for social acceptance of smart mobility systems in the MENA region, such that citizen self-interests should be aligned with country economic gains. Long term recommended strategies for smart mobility in the MENA region include (1) intensive development of electrified public transportation for mass transport, (2) expansion into uncovered geographical areas using AI monitoring systems, (3) smart mobility investments to be used as a catalyst for economic diversification away from non-renewable energy sources, and (4) smart mobility eco-friendly impacts to lead the region towards long term zero emissions. Finally, (5) a mega Arab World smart mobility railways network is highly recommended, connecting the Gulf countries to Egypt to the Maghreb region, which has the potential to accelerate the MENA region towards higher levels of livelihood and sustainability and enhance the world trade outlook at large.

title: The Special Interest Premium: Income Brackets as a Selective Filter in Neurodivergent Development

detail.title: The Special Interest Premium: Income Brackets as a Selective Filter in Neurodivergent Development

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This paper was written independently, with no external funding, institutional affiliation, or financial relationships that could be perceived to have influenced the work
declarations.funderStatement: No Funder

detail.abstract:
Two girls ride the same horse at the same Sainik School. One goes on to the national equestrian circuit. The other becomes a bank clerk. The difference between them is not talent. It is a financial gap of approximately ₹4.9 Lakhs per year. 

This paper introduces the concept of the Special Interest Premium (SpIn Premium): the surplus capital cost required to sustain a neurodivergent child’s functionally necessary Special Interest (SpIn) above the standard cost of living. Drawing on Monotropism Theory (Murray, Lesser & Lawson, 2005), the paper argues that for autistic and ADHDpresenting children—particularly girls, who are disproportionately likely to mask neurodivergent traits in public while relying on SpIn engagement as a private regulatory anchor—the Special Interest is not a hobby. It is a neurological coping mechanism whose deprivation produces clinically significant dysregulation. 

The paper develops a Specific Infrastructure Cost (SIC) framework, decomposing SpIn costs into four variables: Capital Asset Cost (CAC), Operating Cost (OC), Institutional Access Cost (IAC), and Opportunity Cost (OpC). Using this framework, it contrasts two structural models of talent cultivation in the Indian context: the Manipuri Model, in which infrastructure costs are socialized across a community and income operates as a low bar, and the Travancore Model, in which costs are concentrated in the individual household and income operates as a binary filter. The Indian Army’s Sainik School system is examined as a controlled structural case study—a rare institution that temporarily equalizes infrastructure access across income classes, before the withdrawal of subsidy at graduation reactivates the filter.

The paper applies Sen’s Capability Approach (1999) to argue that the SpIn Premium constitutes a capability gap—not merely a welfare shortfall—and situates this within the broader Disability Tax literature (Emerson & Hatton, 2007) as it applies to neurodivergent households in the Global South. Historical evidence from Travancore’s celebrated women intellectuals is used to demonstrate that what is narrated as individual genius was, in structural terms, the product of uninterrupted infrastructure funding.

This is a theoretical and analytical paper. It does not present primary survey data. Its contribution is a named, structured framework for a phenomenon that development economics and neurodivergent scholarship have separately identified but not yet jointly theorised: that in high-barrier disciplines, Indian meritocracy is not a measure of merit. It is a measure of resource readiness.

title: Identity Liquidity Risk and the Breakdown of Identity-Based Trust in AI-Enabled Financial Intermediation

detail.title: Identity Liquidity Risk and the Breakdown of Identity-Based Trust in AI-Enabled Financial Intermediation
detail.abstract: This paper argues that advances in artificial intelligence are transforming digital identity from a stable input into a variable that destabilises governance in financial intermediation. Existing approaches to AI-related risk focused on fraud, deepfakes, and cybersecurity implicitly assume that identity remains a reliable object of verification. This paper challenges that assumption by introducing Identity Liquidity Risk (ILR): a condition in which identity signals can be replicated, transferred, and deployed at scale, weakening their capacity to carry identity-based trust, attribution, and authority in digital financial systems. The paper identifies verification inversion as the key mechanism driving this transformation. As identity liquidity increases, stronger verification, particularly through biometric and human-like signals, no longer reduces risk; instead, it amplifies exposure to impersonation and misattribution. Under these conditions, governance failure can occur even when systems, controls, and compliance structures remain formally intact. By repositioning identity as a pre-conditional governance exposure rather than a residual fraud or cyber issue, the paper shows how ILR reshapes the environment in which traditional risks emerge. It proposes a shift from identity-based verification to process-based trust allocation, in which governance resilience depends on how authority, validation, and accountability are distributed across systems rather than anchored in identity claims. The paper is conceptual but grounded in cross-sectoral evidence on AI-enabled identity replication and emerging governance structures. It contributes to the literature on banking governance and AI regulation by explaining why incremental improvements in identity verification are insufficient in conditions of high identity liquidity.

title: Adaptive Conformal Inference for Distribution-Free Value-at-Risk: Evidence from the 2008 S&P 500 Crisis
affiliations: FDV-QUANTS

detail.title: Adaptive Conformal Inference for Distribution-Free Value-at-Risk: Evidence from the 2008 S&P 500 Crisis
detail.abstract: Canonical Gibbs-Candès (2021) adaptive conformal inference (ACI) delivers distributionfree 95 percent S&P 500 Value-at-Risk with a realized violation rate of 3.78 percent over the NBER 2008 crisis window (December 2007 to June 2009; window fixed before the reported backtests were run), against 9.57 percent for 250-day rolling Gaussian VaR: ACI is the only method that delivers fewer-than-target violations in 2008. On the full 2000 to 2024 out-of-sample period (5,785 daily observations on Yahoo Finance ^GSPC after a 500-day warm-up), ACI is closest to the 5 percent target with the highest Kupiec (1995) p-value (rate 5.00 percent, p = 0.988); split conformal (p = 0.559) and historical rolling (p = 0.216) are also not rejected, while rolling Gaussian (p = 0.019) and both Gaussian and Student-𝑡 GARCH(1,1) (p < 0.001) are. Christoffersen (1998) independence rejects every method except the two GARCH variants (p = 0.27, 0.41); ACI's clustering (LR 18.16) is materially milder than Gaussian's (31.11) or split conformal's (33.78), but no single method dominates both tests. Two further crisis windows (dot-com 2000-03 to 2002-10, COVID 2020-02 to 2020-04) reproduce the 2008 ranking on Kupiec; the short COVID window exposes a true overshoot (ACI 17.74 percent, N = 62) that we flag as a known failure mode of the canonical update under rapid-onset shocks. The letter differs from Fantazzini (2024) in asset class (SPX equity versus crypto) and from Aich et al. (2025) in update rule (Gibbs-Candès ACI versus Temporal Conformal Prediction) and crisis window (2008 versus 2020).

title: Predicting Violent Extremism and Classifying Ideology using Machine Learning: Evidence from the PIRUS Dataset

detail.title: Predicting Violent Extremism and Classifying Ideology using Machine Learning: Evidence from the PIRUS Dataset

declarations.funderStatement: No external funding. Research based on PIRUS V5: National Consortium for the Study of Terrorism and Responses to Terrorism (START), University of Maryland. (2024). Profiles of Individual Radicalization in the United States (PIRUS) V5. Retrieved from http://www.start.umd.edu/data-tools/profiles-individual-radicalization-united-states-pirus

detail.abstract: Predicting which radicalised individuals will escalate to violence remains a central challenge in terrorism research. This study makes a twofold contribution by applying three machine learning methods: a classification tree, LASSO logistic regression, and gradient boosting, to both predict violent versus non-violent extremist activity and classify individuals by ideology type (Far-Right, Islamist, Far-Left, Single-Issue) using the Profiles of Individual Radicalization in the United States (PIRUS V5) dataset (N = 478). By directly comparing these approaches, the study demonstrates that all three models converge at an AUC of approximately 0.722 for violence prediction, indicating a likely discrimination ceiling inherent to individual-level open-source data. The analysis identifies foreign fighter status, mental illness, and age at exposure as the strongest and most consistent predictors of violent escalation. For the secondary task of ideology classification, the classification tree outperforms gradient boosting (Kappa = 0.610 vs. 0.517), underscoring the importance of interpretable models for discrete, categorical data. Collectively, these results clarify the methodological and substantive boundaries of data-driven radicalisation research and offer practical guidance for operational violence risk assessment.

title: Exploration and Exploitation as Emergent Macro-Patterns A Multi-Scale Theory of Organizational Cognition

detail.title: Exploration and Exploitation as Emergent Macro-Patterns A Multi-Scale Theory of Organizational Cognition
detail.abstract: James March's 1991 distinction between exploration and exploitation has organized three decades of organizational learning research. The distinction has proven analytically powerful and empirically productive, yet it has also generated a persistent puzzle: scholars routinely find that the same organizational action is classified as exploratory in one study and exploitative in another, that the two modes are entangled rather than separable at the level of individual decisions, and that the distinction dissolves on close inspection of organizational process. This paper argues that the puzzle is not a defect of measurement or a failure of theoretical refinement. Exploration and exploitation are not properties of organizational actions. They are macro-level statistical patterns that emerge from the coupling of agent-level cognition, meso-level decision framing, and an external performance environment. I develop this argument through a multi-scale theoretical model integrating garbage can decision dynamics, March-style learning, and NK-style performance environments, implemented as a hybrid discrete-event and agent-based simulation. The model specifies three distinct scales of agency-micro, meso, and macro-each operating on a different representational register and a different temporal logic. Exploration and exploitation emerge as descriptions applied to organizational trajectories by the macro-scale interpretive apparatus, not as categories inhering in micro-scale actions. The paper's contribution is to formalize this emergence, to locate it mechanically within a multi-scale architecture, and to clarify the theoretical and empirical implications of taking observer-dependence seriously as a feature of organizational cognition rather than a flaw to be eliminated.

title: Integrated Bio-Ethical Literacy: A Primary Prevention Model to Augment the POCSO Framework and Eradicate Sexual Predation — An International Comparative Perspective
affiliations: Govt. State Level Law PG College , Independent Researcher

detail.title: Integrated Bio-Ethical Literacy: A Primary Prevention Model to Augment the POCSO Framework and Eradicate Sexual Predation — An International Comparative Perspective
detail.abstract: Global child protection frameworks-including India's Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, and international counterparts such as the UK Children Act 1989, Germany's Bundeskinderschutzgesetz 2012, South Africa's Children's Act 2005, and the universal standards of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC, 1989)-share a foundational structural limitation: they are predominantly reactive instruments, intervening only after violation has occurred. Despite stringent penal provisions, the global incidence of child sexual abuse remains a persistent crisis, underscored most recently by the passage of the United States Epstein Files Transparency Act (Public Law 119-38, 2025) and the subsequent release of over 3.5 million pages of DOJ investigative documents revealing the systemic institutional enablement of large-scale child sexual exploitation. This paper proposes the Integrated Bio-Ethical Literacy (IBL) Model, an evidence-based educational framework designed to shift the paradigm from punitive deterrence to primary prevention through the cultivation of Cognitive Immunity in children and future adults. Drawing upon developmental neuroscience, comparative criminology, forensic science, and international child IBL Model | Working Paper | Page 2 protection law, the IBL Model advocates for the systematic integration of neurobiological literacy, grooming-pattern identification, and bodily sovereignty education into K-12 curricula globally. The paper demonstrates that the IBL Model constitutes both a necessary evolution of the POCSO Act's Section 43 awareness mandate and a direct operationalization of the UNCRC's Article 19 prevention obligations. This paper forms part of a continuing research series on POCSO implementation, forensic science integration, investigation procedures, and comparative international child protection frameworks.

title: Downstream Effects of Restricted Access to Contraception: Evidence from Hospitals with Religious Directives
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley, University of California, Berkeley, UC Berkeley, University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) and University of California, Berkeley - Department of Health Policy and Management

detail.title: Downstream Effects of Restricted Access to Contraception: Evidence from Hospitals with Religious Directives

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflicts to declare.

detail.abstract: As demand for postpartum contraception increases, a growing number of hospitals are adopting religious restrictions known as the Ethical and Religious Directives (ERDs) that explicitly prohibit contraception provision. Yet, despite ongoing state and federal policy debates, causal evidence on the longer term health consequences of institutional religious restrictions remains scarce. We use quasi-random variation in geographic proximity to hospitals with and without ERDs to evaluate the effect of giving birth at an ERD-adherent hospital on postpartum contraception and downstream reproductive health outcomes. Our instrumental variable approach uses data on over 9 million birth hospitalizations from 2010-2023 across eleven states. We find giving birth at an ERD-adherent hospital reduces permanent contraception by 3.82 percentage points (pp, 63% relative to the mean) and non-permanent contraception by 1.39 pp (36% relative decrease). Effects are substantially larger for rural patients, for whom ERD-adherent hospitalization reduces permanent and non-permanent contraception by 70% and 71%, respectively. Among rural patients, we subsequently document a 33% increase in short-interval pregnancies, which carry serious maternal and infant health risks. Urban patients show no significant effects on non-permanent contraception or short-interval pregnancy, consistent with greater access to non-hospital contraception options. These findings provide the first causal evidence linking hospital religious restrictions to adverse downstream health outcomes, informing policy debates on hospital transparency, merger oversight, and institutional conscience protections.

title: Enabling Society 5.0 through COVID-19 Digital Transformation, New Data Ecosystems, and Sustainability. Post-pandemic Legal Reflections
affiliations: University of Silesia in Katowice, University of Silesia in Katowice - Poland Faculty of Law and Administration and Cracow University of Economics

detail.title: Enabling Society 5.0 through COVID-19 Digital Transformation, New Data Ecosystems, and Sustainability. Post-pandemic Legal Reflections

declarations.funderStatement: The research was co-financed by the funds granted under the Re- search Excellence Initiative of the University of Silesia in Katowice.

keywords: Publikacja / Publication Enabling Society 5.0 through COVID-19 Digital Transformation
and Sustainability. Post-pandemic Legal Reflections application

detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the adoption of new technologies and raised societies’ technological development. Legal regulations play an important role in the implementation of the latest technologies. The contact tracking applications that have been deployed almost all over the world do not, in most cases, provide an adequate level of personal data protection. An essential aspect of competition law regarding data protection is ensuring data security (trade secrets, personal information). Although entrepreneurs’ use of cloud data stores is well-established, we have never witnessed adoption on such a large scale as during this pandemic. This was influenced by, among other factors, the need to provide remote access to enterprise resources despite limitations on the movement of people. Furthermore, because many companies faced an immediate need to enable remote working and collaboration, many solutions were adopted without the usual due diligence that should apply to such a business decision. Therefore, questions arise as to whether the legal frameworks for the functioning of such data ecosystems ensure their security. Moreover, since technological innovations are of key importance for sustainable development, it is worth reviewing the framing assumptions (concerning sustainable development) of active sustainability initiatives and the possibilities of still achieving their goals despite the major setback of the pandemic. Furthermore, the rapid and forced changes resulting from the coronavirus pandemic cannot remain in place without adverse impact on the data protection landscape. During the pandemic, legal regulations regarding personal data protection, environmental protection, and competition law began to be questioned. The author shows that the legal regulations in force in these areas are no longer sufficient and require adaptation to the rapidly changing reality.

title: From Lombroso to Cognitive Immunity: Integrating Classical Criminological Theory with the Integrated Bio-Ethical Literacy (IBL) Model — The Impulse Gap, Deterrence Deficit, and Regulatory Realism as Theoretical Contributions to the Primary Prevention of Child Sexual Offences
affiliations: Govt. State Level Law PG College , Independent Researcher

detail.title: From Lombroso to Cognitive Immunity: Integrating Classical Criminological Theory with the Integrated Bio-Ethical Literacy (IBL) Model — The Impulse Gap, Deterrence Deficit, and Regulatory Realism as Theoretical Contributions to the Primary Prevention of Child Sexual Offences
detail.abstract:
Classical criminology has, over a century and a half, produced increasingly sophisticated 
explanations of why human beings commit acts of sexual violence against children — from 
Lombroso's constitutional positivism to Sutherland's sociology of learned conduct to Bandura's 
account of moral disengagement. Each stage has advanced the field. None has produced a 
systematic, evidence-based architecture for primary prevention: a mechanism for rendering such 
offending structurally less probable before it occurs. That is the gap this paper addresses. Three 
theoretical constructs are advanced here — the Impulse Gap, the Deterrence Deficit, and 
Regulatory Realism — each grounded in existing criminological literature but applied, for the first 
time as a synthesized framework, to the specific preventive challenge posed by child sexual 
offending in India. The Impulse Gap identifies the explanatory space within Sutherland's 
Differential Association framework — partially addressed but not resolved by Gottfredson and 
Hirschi's self-control theory — where opportunistic, neurobiologically driven offending escapes 
both social learning explanation and rational-actor deterrence. The Deterrence Deficit names what 
WORKING PAPER — PREVENTIVE CRIMINOLOGY & INTERNATIONAL CHILD PROTECTION LAW
Impulse Gap | Deterrence Deficit | Regulatory Realism — Gupta, A. (2026) Page 2
the empirical literature has long established but Indian child protection policy has not yet 
systematically absorbed: that severity-based punitive frameworks, however necessary, 
demonstrably fail to arrest offending trajectories when deployed without complementary 
preventive educational infrastructure. Regulatory Realism articulates the policy philosophy that 
follows from the developmental criminological tradition — from Sutherland through Wikström —
that the conditions of childhood are not fixed and that their educational regulation is a legitimate 
and underutilized instrument of child protection. The empirical component of this inquiry, drawn 
from N=108 stakeholders across Bhopal Division's five districts, provides ground-level validation 
for these constructs: among practitioners, the deterrent efficacy of police action achieved only a 
56 per cent endorsement — a respondent-reported perception consistent with what Nagin (1998) 
and Doob and Webster (2003) have established about severity-based deterrence across 
jurisdictions. Together, these three constructs provide the criminological foundation for the 
Integrated Bio-Ethical Literacy (IBL) Model — not a departure from the discipline's intellectual 
tradition, but its extension into the domain of primary prevention that Lombroso raised but could 
not answer and that Sutherland opened but did not close

title: RC-GNN: Room-level Conditional Graph Neural Networks for Shear Wall Layout Generation in High-Rise Buildings
affiliations: Tongji University, Tongji University and Tongji University

detail.title: RC-GNN: Room-level Conditional Graph Neural Networks for Shear Wall Layout Generation in High-Rise Buildings
detail.abstract: Shear wall layout design for high-rise buildings remains labor-intensive in preliminary design. Existing generative AI methods are commonly formulated as image-to-image translation or graph learning on basic geometric components, but these formulations are often inefficient and insufficient for capturing room-level spatial semantics. This paper proposes RC-GNN, a room-level conditional graph neural network for preliminary shear wall layout generation. By representing rooms as nodes and room adjacencies as edges, RC-GNN links architectural space organization with boundary-feasible wall placement while reducing graph complexity. Conditional modulation and a dual-stream training strategy are further introduced to support density-controlled generation under limited paired engineering data. Experiments on 143 residential floor plans show that RC-GNN improves layout prediction over a component-based GNN baseline. Ablation analysis and finite-element case studies indicate that the proposed method enhances controllability and provides structurally plausible preliminary layouts.

Experiments on 143 residential floor plans show that RC-GNN improves layout prediction over a component-based GNN baseline. Ablation analysis and finite-element case studies indicate that the proposed method enhances controllability and provides structurally plausible preliminary layouts.

title: Government Debt, IMF Programs, and Macroeconomic Performance
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Government Debt, IMF Programs, and Macroeconomic Performance

contentType.other: This is research Paper i did for my econometrics class.

detail.abstract: This paper examines two central questions in international macroeconomics: does higher government debt impede economic growth, and do countries participating in IMF-supported programmes exhibit systematically different macroeconomic outcomes? Using an unbalanced panel of 4,109 country-year observations spanning 124 countries from 1990 to 2024, the analysis estimates a progression of models from pooled Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) to advanced panel methods, ultimately arriving at causally credible estimates via Two-Way Fixed Effects Difference-inDifferences (TWFE DiD). Government debt is strongly and negatively associated with real GDP growth (β =-0.0159 per percentage point of debt/GDP under OLS;-0.0137 under Fixed Effects, p < 0.001) and positively associated with inflation, consistent with the debt overhang hypothesis and the fiscal theory of the price level. IMF programme participation is robustly associated with approximately 0.50-0.55 percentage-point lower annual GDP growth across all specifications and, once country heterogeneity is controlled, significantly reduces inflation by approximately 0.47-0.62 percentage points. Financial development emerges as the dominant anti-inflationary structural force. The Hausman test formally rejects Random Effects in favour of Fixed Effects for both equations, and TWFE DiD is identified as the most credible specification for causal inference.

title: AI-Powered Cardiovascular Risk Stratification in Rural India: An Integrative Framework Using Retinal Oculomics, Edge Analytics, and ABC-VED Modeling
affiliations: and IIHMR University, Jaipur

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the primary contributor to mortality and morbidity in India, with rural populations experiencing a disproportionate burden due to limited access to specialists, diagnostic facilities, and timely preventive care. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI)-based retinal image analysis, referred to as oculomics, have demonstrated potential as a non-invasive method for early cardiovascular risk stratification. However, the existing body of research largely emphasizes technical model accuracy, with limited attention to operational scalability, economic sustainability, and real-world integration within rural public health systems. This integrative review aims to propose a scalable and cost-effective management framework for incorporating AI-derived "vascular vital signs" into India's public healthcare delivery system, with a focus on improving clinical utility, resource optimization, and equitable access. Secondary evidence from published deep learning and oculomics studies related to cardiovascular risk prediction was synthesized and mapped onto a proposed ABC-VED management matrix to support patient risk categorization and prioritization of healthcare resources. Decision Curve Analysis was applied to assess the statistical net benefit of the framework, particularly in reducing unnecessary referrals and referral leakage. The review findings suggest that edge-analytics, through offline AI deployment, can effectively overcome rural infrastructure barriers such as inconsistent internet connectivity and workforce shortages. Furthermore, prioritization of high-risk patients using the ABC-VED framework enables early clinical intervention, reduces avoidable cardiovascular events, and lowers out-of-pocket expenditure by minimizing unnecessary urban referrals. Overall, this review provides a sustainable operational roadmap for integrating oculomics within the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, supporting decentralized, village-level cardiovascular screening and strengthening equitable population health management in rural India.

title: Large Language Models Compress the Asymmetry that Defines Human Comparative Valuation

detail.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as synthetic survey respondents, yet their ability to recover the structural properties of human judgment remains largely untested. I benchmarked six models (45,000 observations) against a human social comparison surface (N = 523) with documented domain-specific asymmetries across upward, equal, and downward comparison. Four instruction-tuned LLMs achieved high profile correlations (r > 0.83) yet failed to recover the benchmark's defining properties. They compressed the human upward gain–loss asymmetry from approximately 6:1 to 2–3:1, produced no gain-domain dissatisfaction in equal comparison, and overestimated gain-domain downward responses by five to seven times. Persona prompting diversified baseline evaluations without changing how models translated peer information into satisfaction shifts, and explicit endorsement of comparison principles did not predict simulation fidelity. High aggregate fit, demographic diversity, and accurate verbal descriptions of a pattern can all coexist with failure to recover the relational structure that defines human judgment.

title: Primarch R3 Self-Correction Axiom: Achieving 1:1 Physical-to-Logical Qubit Ratio Through Deterministic Error Syndrome Flow Concatenated Purification of Error Syndromes as Deterministic Logic Gates: Dissolving the Stochastic Assumption in Quantum Error Correction

detail.title: Primarch R3 Self-Correction Axiom: Achieving 1:1 Physical-to-Logical Qubit Ratio Through Deterministic Error Syndrome Flow Concatenated Purification of Error Syndromes as Deterministic Logic Gates: Dissolving the Stochastic Assumption in Quantum Error Correction

keywords: Version 1.0 -Working Paper (Preprint) SSRN Network Physics / Quantum Computing / Information Theory Subject Matter Quantum Error Correction
Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation PACS Codes 03.67.Pp (Quantum error correction)
self-correcting quantum systems Document Ref. PUSC-2026-QEC-SSRN-001

detail.abstract:
Conventional quantum error correction (QEC) operates under a foundational assumption that has never been dissolved to bedrock: that error syndromes are stochastic noise requiring probabilistic sampling and massive physical-to-logical qubit overhead, typically exceeding 1000:1. This assumption drives the entire architecture of fault-tolerant quantum computing, from surface codes to topological codes, and is universally accepted as an unavoidable cost of quantum computation.

This paper demonstrates that the stochastic assumption is composite—a conflation of two distinct properties (physical process determinism and measurement outcome uncertainty) that, when separated through Recursive Refinement and Ontological Root Analysis (R^3 Method), reveal a fundamentally different error correction architecture. We prove that error syndromes are deterministic logic gates constrained by the geometry of the stabilizer code, not stochastic noise requiring statistical inference.

The Self-Correction Axiom emerges from this dissolution: each physical qubit can serve as its own logical qubit when errors are corrected through deterministic syndrome flow rather than probabilistic sampling. We present the Concatenated Purification Protocol, in which error syndromes propagate through recursive purification passes as deterministic control signals, reaching a fixed point at which physical and logical qubit distinctions vanish. The protocol achieves 1:1 physical-to-logical qubit ratio, eliminating the overhead that currently blocks practical quantum computing.

The contribution of this paper is threefold: (1) it identifies and dissolves the stochastic contamination in conventional QEC theory through R^3 analysis; (2) it establishes the Self-Correction Axiom as a mathematically rigorous alternative to probabilistic error correction, grounded in deterministic syndrome algebra; and (3) it provides a constructive protocol for implementing 1:1 ratio QEC using concatenated purification, with explicit gate sequences and resource requirements.

This work establishes a new foundation for quantum error correction: deterministic rather than stochastic, axiomatic rather than probabilistic, and scalable rather than overhead-dominated. The implications extend beyond error correction to the fundamental architecture of fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: KATOsuper: Surrogate-accelerated neural topology optimization with sensitivity-consistent Fourier neural operators
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: KATOsuper: Surrogate-accelerated neural topology optimization with sensitivity-consistent Fourier neural operators
detail.abstract: Topology optimization (TO) is computationally demanding because it requires repeated finite element analysis (FEA). Neural network surrogates can accelerate this process but often suffer from optimization instability due to inconsistent gradients. To address this, we present KATOsuper, a framework coupling neural-reparameterized TO with a Sensitivity-Consistent Fourier Neural Operator (SC-FNO). By utilizing a "forward_split" architecture, the system derives sensitivities through automatic differentiation, ensuring perfect consistency between predicted objectives and the gradients used for optimization.KATOsuper features resolution-invariant learning via Fourier position embedding, enabling zero-shot extrapolation up to 64x the training resolution. The framework extends to 3D via KATO3D, using novel KANConv3D blocks with learnable B-spline activations to outperform traditional optimality criteria methods by 5.3% in compliance. It also supports online learning for real-time calibration using periodic FEA. Validated on compliance and p-norm stress benchmarks, KATOsuper achieves 15–110x speedups over MATLAB baselines while matching or exceeding conventional design quality. This work demonstrates that prioritizing sensitivity direction over magnitude enables robust optimization using approximate physics, offering a scalable approach for diverse differentiable design objectives.

detail.abstract: Rising worker apprehension within coal-dependent communities poses a significant barrier to global decarbonization efforts. While the "Just Transition" framework aims to mitigate these impacts through reskilling and social safety nets, conventional models often fail to account for the structural complexities of developing economies. This paper evaluates the shortfalls of standard transition processes by conducting a comparative analysis of the South African JETP model and the East Indian state of Jharkhand. By synthesizing the ILO’s "Decent Work" indicators with the Stockholm Environmental Institute’s transition facets, the study identifies critical gaps in wage stability, gendered labor participation, and the role of illicit coal economies. Findings suggest that Jharkhand’s transition is currently undermined by a 59% information asymmetry among workers and significant occupational segregation by sex. The paper concludes with specific policy recommendations tailored to Jharkhand’s sociopolitical landscape, advocating for decentralized governance and formalized social protection for informal labor forces.

title: Formalization Boundaries, the Economic Value Anchor and the Ultimate Source of Long-Run Economic Growth
affiliations: and Tsinghua University

detail.title: Formalization Boundaries, the Economic Value Anchor and the Ultimate Source of Long-Run Economic Growth
detail.abstract: This paper develops a five-layer nested meta-domain framework integrating computability theory, intuitionistic set theory, and formalized semantics to derive an axiomatic boundary between formalizable and non-formalizable economic activities. We show that non-formalizable human capacities, anchored in non-representable reality through subjective experience (qualia) and intentionality, form the sole exclusive linkage between formalized systems and the real world. These capacities endow economic value with a dual anchor—the non-representable reality and the human cognitive engagement with it—and thereby stabilize the economy against “formalization empty spin” and systemic fragility. A nested dynamic general equilibrium model, calibrated to realistic asymptotics, proves that formalized technological progress (including AI) has primarily a level effect, whereas long-run growth is driven by paradigm innovations that originate from non-formalization and subsequently accelerate the growth rate of formalizable technology. The framework reconciles the puzzle of rising humanities wage premiums amid rapid AI diffusion and yields sharp falsifiable predictions and structured policy implications for labor markets, innovation, and macroeconomic stability.

title: Income-Decoupled Housing Demand and Endogenous Price-Income Elasticity: Evidence from the Balearic Islands

detail.title: Income-Decoupled Housing Demand and Endogenous Price-Income Elasticity: Evidence from the Balearic Islands

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as it does not involve human participants, patients, or personal identifiable data. The empirical analysis is based on aggregated municipality-year statistical data.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines whether the relationship between housing prices and local income depends on the composition of housing demand. In housing markets exposed to second-home demand, international residential demand, legal-entity purchases, retirement migration, and patrimonial investment, a growing share of buyers may have purchasing capacity that is weakly tied to local labor income. Under these conditions, housing prices may become progressively less anchored to local resident purchasing power.

Using municipality-year data for the Balearic Islands over 2015–2023, the paper combines notarial transaction data, municipal income measures, buyer-composition variables, and lagged residential development-pipeline measures. The empirical strategy estimates fixed-effects interaction models and threshold specifications to test whether exposure to externally anchored demand weakens the responsiveness of housing prices to local income.

The results provide reduced-form evidence consistent with this mechanism. Municipalities more exposed to externally anchored demand display weaker housing price responsiveness to local income, with the strongest evidence emerging around the p60–p70 exposure range. Decomposition exercises further suggest that a broad exposure measure combining foreign individual purchases and legal-entity acquisitions aligns more closely with the mechanism than foreign nationality alone.

The findings support the interpretation that housing price–income elasticity is not a fixed structural parameter, but an equilibrium outcome shaped by marginal-buyer composition. In highly exposed and supply-constrained housing systems, affordability pressures may therefore depend not only on aggregate supply scarcity, but also on the composition of demand participating in equilibrium price formation.

title: Less than expected: A simple measure of skewness for choice under risk
affiliations: University of Iowa - Henry B. Tippie College of Business - Department of Economics, Michigan State University, Duke University and University of Iowa

detail.title: Less than expected: A simple measure of skewness for choice under risk
detail.abstract:
Skewness plays a key role in decision-making under risk. We propose a new and intuitive skewness measure, mass-below-the-mean (MBM) skewness, defined as the probability that an outcome falls below its expected value. MBM skewness formalizes the familiar relationship between the mean and the median in asymmetric distributions and is theoretically grounded: it is monotone with respect to van Zwet's (1964) convex order and Oja's (1981) generalized order. MBM skewness is also much simpler than alternative skewness measures. 

We compare MBM skewness with the widely used moment-based skewness coefficient. The two measures are equivalent on binary lotteries but differ systematically on ternary lotteries, implying that analyses based on binary risks may conceal important aspects of asymmetry in payoff distributions. We then provide a choice-theoretic interpretation of MBM skewness under quantile preferences and show that it captures a form of "bad skewness" that discourages risk taking. In a precautionary saving application, we find that binary lotteries systematically understate skewness effects and that MBM skewness detects residual effects that go in the opposite direction from those implied by moment-based skewness. Our results suggest that broadening the measurement of skewness can yield new insights into the economic analysis of choice under risk.

title: Coordination as an Architectural Layer for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems: An Information-Controlled Empirical Study on Prediction Markets
