title: Less Volume, More Variety: An Inverse Relationship Between LLM Output Length and Contrarian Discovery in Pharmaceutical Stock Selection
affiliations: Betalabs Inc

detail.title: Less Volume, More Variety: An Inverse Relationship Between LLM Output Length and Contrarian Discovery in Pharmaceutical Stock Selection

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests. The author holds no equity, options, or other financial positions in the pharmaceutical companies referenced in this study, and has no financial relationship or consulting arrangement with any of the four large language model providers analyzed (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek). No external funding was received for this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The author conducted the study independently using publicly accessible web interfaces of the four large language models analyzed.

detail.abstract: We report preliminary evidence of a counterintuitive empirical pattern in large language model (LLM) based equity research: shorter outputs contain proportionally more contrarian stock recommendations than longer ones. Submitting an identical pharmaceutical sector long/short prompt to four frontier LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini) on May 4, 2026, we observe a strong negative rank correlation (Spearman ρ = −0.80 across all four models; ρ = −1.00 when ChatGPT — identified as a stale-data outlier — is excluded) between output length and what we term the contrarian discovery rate — the count of unique stock picks not appearing in any other model's recommendation, normalized by output length. The most compressed model (Gemini, 4.13 KB) generated 14 times more contrarian picks per kilobyte than the most verbose (DeepSeek, 38.6 KB). We propose a compression-forces-selection mechanism: when token budget is constrained, models cannot afford to enumerate consensus picks and must allocate scarce capacity to differentiated signals. Given the small sample (n = 4) and single-period design, we frame the result as a hypothesis-generating observation, and outline a five-study research agenda for causal identification, scaled replication, and forward performance evaluation.

title: A Structural Resolution of the Easterlin Paradox: Why Income Does and Does Not Buy Happiness

detail.title: A Structural Resolution of the Easterlin Paradox: Why Income Does and Does Not Buy Happiness
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a structural resolution of the Easterlin Paradox by decomposing utility into distinct underlying mechanisms through which wealth generates well-being. Building on a unified framework, total utility is expressed as the sum of experiential and relational components, which are further decomposed into Relief, Comfort, Status, and Achievement Utility. These components differ in their marginal properties, reference points, and aggregate implications. The analysis shows that the Easterlin Paradox arises naturally from the internal composition of utility rather than from a contradiction between absolute and relative income effects. At the individual level, higher income increases well-being through improvements in lived conditions, relative position, and progress toward personal benchmarks. At the aggregate level, however, common income growth produces attenuated gains because the high-marginal-value experiential component diminishes with wealth, while status-based utility depends on relative position and does not scale with overall income. The framework reconciles empirical findings that have traditionally been viewed as competing, including positive cross-sectional income gradients and weak long-run relationships between income and average well-being. It also generates testable predictions regarding the composition of income effects, including the declining importance of deprivation-related factors and the increasing importance of relative position across the wealth distribution. More broadly, the paper contributes a mechanism-based interpretation of the income-well-being relationship that integrates insights from subjective well-being research, social comparison theory, and behavioral economics within a single coherent model.

title: Predicting the Unpredictable: Representativeness Bias and Speculative Trading in Stock Market
affiliations: University of International Business and Economics (UIBE) - Business School, City University of Hong Kong (CityU) and Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Business

detail.title: Predicting the Unpredictable: Representativeness Bias and Speculative Trading in Stock Market
detail.abstract: This paper explores how representativeness bias triggers speculative trading in financial markets, leading to distortions in asset prices. Using the unique stock split mechanism in China, we identify a key representative feature, "split source," a combination of retained earnings and capital reserves that investors use for predicting stock splits. We show that investors heuristically associate the size of the split source with the likelihood and magnitude of a stock split, overlooking the fact that firms rarely do stock splits based solely on the split source. This erroneous belief drives speculative trading, as investors target stocks with high ex-ante split sources, resulting in significant price run-ups before the announcement of contingent stock splits, followed by complete reversal afterward. The return pattern is robust across various research designs and robustness checks, and is more pronounced for smaller stocks, stocks with higher illiquidity and lower institutional ownership. Additional evidence from retail investor buying demand and posts on social media further supports the idea that retail investors' beliefs about the likelihood of stock splits are indeed influenced by split source.

title: From Social Acceptance to Well-Being: A Capability Approach to Wind Power Policy in Norway
affiliations: University of Oslo, University of Oslo, University of Oslo, University of Oslo, University of Oslo and University of Oslo

detail.title: From Social Acceptance to Well-Being: A Capability Approach to Wind Power Policy in Norway

declarations.funderStatement: The study was supported by the European Union’s Horizon Europe research and innovation programme project SAMVIND (Grant 101061882).

detail.abstract: Using the Capability Approach, this paper examines how people's aspirations shape their perceptions of wind energy development in two Norwegian municipalities, Aremark and Båtsfjord. We situate the study within critical debates on social acceptance of renewable energy technologies (RETs), arguing that dominant techno-economic and "fix-oriented" approaches overlook how energy infrastructures affect multidimensional well-being, justice and everyday life in specific places. Empirically, we draw on semi-structured interviews and focus groups with 58 participants, including residents, municipal representatives, industry actors, NGOs and Sámi reindeer herders. The research design combines a grounded, participatory methodology with collective analysis and explicit attention to positionality, power relations and community involvement. Using a description-grounded operationalisation of the Capability Approach, we identify locally defined "elements of a good life" and examine how wind energy projects may enhance or constrain people's capabilities to realise them. Three shared well-being dimensions emerge: (1) being able to live in and care for a clean, accessible natural environment; (2) having financial security and meaningful work; and (3) maintaining close relations with family and friends. The analysis shows that a capability-based, bottom-up approach can enrich energy debates by making visible locally defined aspirations, relational and more-than-human dimensions of well-being, and tensions between environmental protection, livelihood security and social cohesion. We argue that wind energy projects in Norway and beyond should be evaluated not only through climate and cost metrics, but also in terms of how they expand or restrict the real opportunities of diverse communities and species to live lives they have reason to value.

title: Pricing Monetary Issuance: Tradable Issuance Rights and Fiscal Revenue
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Pricing Monetary Issuance: Tradable Issuance Rights and Fiscal Revenue

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is theoretical and does not involve human subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
I propose a mechanism of Tradable Issuance Rights (TIR) for monetary issuance, in which the right to create base money is treated as a tradable institutional asset. Monetary issuance in this paper refers exclusively to the issuance of base money, rather than bank deposit creation through lending. Within this framework, TIR are allocated via market-based auctions, capitalizing seigniorage into explicit institutional revenue and thereby enhancing fiscal capacity without expanding public debt. Both the equilibrium quantity and price of TIR are endogenously determined by banks’ funding costs and lending returns.

The model shows that partially decentralizing monetary TIR from the central authority—thereby constraining the government’s monetary power—can enhance fiscal capacity. The TIR mechanism transforms monetary issuance from the policy instrument into a market-determined outcome, thereby linking the creation of base money directly to underlying economic fundamentals. In addition, the sale of TIR generates non-debt fiscal revenue, linking government financing capacity to underlying credit market returns and inducing automatic contraction in low-return states. The model further shows that the TIR mechanism improves allocative efficiency and transforms implicit seigniorage into explicit fiscal revenue.

Overall, I provide a unified analytical framework in which monetary issuance, fiscal capacity, and financial intermediation are jointly and endogenously determined within a single-currency system.

title: A Comparative Analysis of Anti-Money Laundering Regimes in the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman Legal Frameworks, Licensed Financial Institutions, and Informal Value Transfer Systems
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Comparative Analysis of Anti-Money Laundering Regimes in the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman Legal Frameworks, Licensed Financial Institutions, and Informal Value Transfer Systems

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patients, or any identifiable living individuals. It relies exclusively on publicly available legislation, court records, scholarly publications, and industry reports. Therefore, no ethics approval or written consent was required.

detail.abstract: Money laundering and terrorist financing remain persistent challenges for Gulf Cooperation Council states. The United Arab Emirates and Oman have developed distinct approaches to combating these threats, shaped by different economic ambitions, regulatory philosophies, and experiences with international pressure. This study compares the two regimes by examining three core areas: the legal and institutional frameworks, the obligations imposed on licensed financial institutions, and the treatment of informal value transfer systems, particularly Hawala. The UAE has pursued an aggressive reform agenda since its 2022-2024 grey-listing by the Financial Action Task Force. Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 and Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025 now provide a comprehensive framework that explicitly criminalises proliferation financing, establishes an operationally independent Financial Intelligence Unit within the Central Bank, and mandates licensing for money or value transfer service providers. The UAE employs tiered customer due diligence thresholds of AED 55,000 for occasional transactions and AED 3,500 for wire transfers. Administrative fines range from AED 10,000 to AED 5,000,000 per violation. Oman continues to operate under Royal Decree No. 30 of 2016, supplemented by guidelines issued by the Central Bank of Oman and the Capital Market Authority. The Omani framework captures Hawala operators under the general definition of financial institutions but lacks a dedicated registration regime. The guidelines establish thresholds of OMR 5,000 for occasional transactions and OMR 350 for wire transfers. Administrative fines range from RO 10,000 to RO 100,000 per violation. Proliferation financing is referenced only in the context of United Nations Security Council resolutions and is not criminalised as a standalone offence. Scholarly research indicates that money exchange providers in both jurisdictions demonstrate low anti-money laundering disclosure levels: approximately 19 per cent in the UAE and 26 per cent in Oman. Omani legislation, while aligned with international standards, faces challenges related to delayed judicial procedures and weak international coordination. The study concludes that the UAE has achieved significant legislative modernisation, but that legislative strength does not automatically translate into effective implementation in either jurisdiction. Oman requires amendments to address proliferation financing explicitly, enhance Financial Intelligence Unit independence, and strengthen enforcement transparency.

title: The Unified Field Theory’s “Thousand-Fold” Day–Night Satellite Clock-Bias Prediction Is Strongly Confirmed by Early Raw Clock Solutions from Multiple Satellite Classes
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Unified Field Theory’s “Thousand-Fold” Day–Night Satellite Clock-Bias Prediction Is Strongly Confirmed by Early Raw Clock Solutions from Multiple Satellite Classes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial or personal conflicts of interest related to this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human subjects. All experiments were conducted in accordance with local regulations on animal welfare and agricultural research practices.

detail.abstract: Using publicly available IGS/MGEX precise clock and orbit products, we audit raw GNSS satellite clock records from BeiDou, GPS, Galileo, and GLONASS prior to the widespread use of the ECOM2 high-order solar radiation pressure model. A robust 24-hour, solar-phase-locked, nanosecond-level diurnal clock signal is consistently observed across multiple satellite types, with peak-to-peak amplitudes far exceeding the solar tidal residuals expected under standard general relativity. By compiling reported datasets, we find an almost perfectly linear scaling of the signal amplitude with geocentric orbital radius, further strengthened by the altitude-dependent behavior of the eccentric-orbit Galileo satellites within the same orbital period. We argue that ECOM2, via multiple empirical parameters, can absorb this periodic structure as “systematic error,” yielding artificially smooth clock series in modern products. These findings provide a reproducible observational testbed for time-potential-based unified-field interpretations and motivate reprocessing strategies that minimize empirical absorption of physically coherent diurnal signatures.

title:
The Displacement Hypothesis

Does Suppression of Consensual Adult Sexual Activity Correlate with Increased Child Sexual Victimisation? A Comparative Empirical Analysis
affiliations: Govt. State Level Law PG College , Independent Researcher

detail.title:
The Displacement Hypothesis

Does Suppression of Consensual Adult Sexual Activity Correlate with Increased Child Sexual Victimisation? A Comparative Empirical Analysis
detail.abstract: Child sexual abuse remains among the most egregious manifestations of predatory human behaviour, yet its structural determinants are seldom examined through the lens of regulatory failure rather than individual pathology alone. This paper advances the Displacement Hypothesis: when legitimate, consensual, and regulated expressions of adult sexuality are systematically suppressed-through criminalisation, social stigma, or institutional prohibition-the resulting demand doesn't extinguish itself; rather, it displaces toward victims who are most structurally vulnerable, including children and non-consenting adults. Drawing on comparative empirical data from six jurisdictions-the Netherlands, New Zealand, Rhode Island (USA), Sweden, Germany, and India-this paper examines documented correlations between the regulatory architecture governing consensual adult sexual activity and the incidence of child sexual victimisation and coercive sexual crime. The analysis is descriptive and comparative; it makes no normative prescription regarding any particular regulatory model, but identifies a significant research gap warranting systematic empirical investigation in the Indian context. The paper integrates three significant bodies of contemporary evidence: the global #MeToo movement (2017-present) as a structural indicator of the pervasive institutional tolerance of sexual harm; the Supreme Court of India's progressive jurisprudence on sex worker dignity in Buddhadev Karmaskar v. State of West Bengal (2011, 2022); and the comparative regulatory evidence from decriminalised jurisdictions. The paper situates this analysis within the broader Regulatory Realism framework developed across the author's prior published works, arguing that any comprehensive primary prevention strategy for child sexual abuse-including the Integrated Bio-Ethical Literacy (IBL) Model proposed in Gupta (2026a)-must account for the structural demand-side dynamics that current Indian law leaves unaddressed.

title: Linking Algal Geochemistry to Biohydrogen Production Potential: A Multi-Technique Assessment of Eutrophic Macroalgae from India
affiliations: University of Petroleum and Energy Studies (UPES), Manipal Institute of Technology,  and University of Petroleum and Energy Studies

detail.title: Linking Algal Geochemistry to Biohydrogen Production Potential: A Multi-Technique Assessment of Eutrophic Macroalgae from India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declares no competing interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Eutrophication-driven macroalgal proliferation in freshwater and coastal systems is simultaneously an environmental burden and an underexploited bioenergy resource. This study, the first of its kind, characterizes eutrophic macroalgal biomass from four geographically distinct Indian sites (two freshwater bodies in Doon Valley, Uttarakhand; two Arabian Sea coastal locations in Kerala and Karnataka) to assess dark fermentation suitability for biohydrogen (H₂) production. Eight samples across five genera (Chaetomorpha, Laurencia, Ulva, Fucus, Oedogonium) were evaluated by proximate analysis, CHNS, XRD, and TGA. XRD revealed environment-specific mineralogical fingerprints: amorphous biogenic silica in Chaetomorpha, crystalline CaCO₃ in Oedogonium, iron oxysulfides in Fucus, and anomalous Bi-Pb sulfides in Laurencia. TGA confirmed multi-step thermal decomposition across all samples, with primary devolatilization between 200-400°C; volatile matter ranged 34.5-74.92% and carbon 20.95-66.35%. Ulva sp. and Fucus sp. emerged as the strongest candidates, combining high volatile matter (59.95-60.37%), favorable carbon content, and mineral assemblages consistent with anaerobic metabolism. The Fe-oxysulfide signature of Fucus sp. is particularly notable as a geochemical proxy for pre-existing reducing conditions analogous to dark fermentation environments. Despite peak volatile matter and carbon values, Laurencia sp. (M6) is predicted to yield negligible H₂ due to hydrogenase inhibition by Bi, Pb, and Cu. Oedogonium showed limited potential from high CaCO₃ loading and suboptimal C/N ratios. All samples fell below the 20-30:1 dark fermentation optimum, making co-substrate supplementation necessary. This work establishes the first direct geochemistry-biohydrogen relationship in eutrophic macroalgal biomass, demonstrating that integrated XRD-TGA-CHNS screening is a more discriminating feedstock evaluation framework than proximate analysis alone.

title: Cyclone Risk and Socioeconomic Vulnerability in Indian Coastal Districts
affiliations: University of Burdwan and University of Burdwan

detail.title: Cyclone Risk and Socioeconomic Vulnerability in Indian Coastal Districts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that there are no conflicts of interest regarding the publication of this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, biological materials, or data. Therefore, ethical approval and consent to participate are not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: No financial support or funding was received for conducting this study.

detail.abstract: The Indian sub-continent especially the coastal part of India is one of the most affected regions due to disasters as it is exposed to nearly 10 percent of the world's tropical cyclone. The assessment of vulnerability is a significant tool for policymakers to prioritize the interventions for adaptive measurements. In this context, it becomes imperative to examine the impact of tropical cyclone on the lives of the people in the coastal districts of India, focusing on education and livelihood. It also explores the intersection of natural hazard vulnerability and socioeconomic vulnerability. The study initially applies regression analysis to examine the impact of cyclone proneness effects on education and livelihood. Further, to check the overlap and identify the districts majorly vulnerable to the compounding effects of tropical cyclones and socioeconomic backwardness several vulnerability indices have been constructed by principal component analysis, and geometric mean. The study reveals higher cyclone intensifying regions experience higher decline in literacy rates, rising number of out-ofschool children, increasing poverty levels, food insecurity, and lowering the average MPCE compare to the low or moderate cyclone-prone areas. Finally, districts showing high coastal vulnerability and needing immediate policy interventions for more equitable development and disaster preparedness have also been identified.

title: The Abductive Hypothesis Engine: Evolving Observational Causal Inference
affiliations: Lead Researcher, o-machine

detail.title: The Abductive Hypothesis Engine: Evolving Observational Causal Inference
detail.abstract:
We propose the Abductive Hypothesis Engine, a structural departure from traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and runtime neuro-symbolic prompting. Current Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with real-world causal inference because they conflate hypothesis generation with verification, relying on fuzzy linguistic semantics that are highly susceptible to hallucination. To address this, our system systematically shifts the burden of causal inference away from LLM text generation and onto deterministic, offline algorithms. The LLM's role is strictly confined to that of a natural language interface (NLI), tasked only with translating formally verified proofs into human-readable text. 
To achieve this, the engine adapts LLM-driven evolutionary coding to evolve constructive graphtraversal algorithms over a rigorous topological graph of discrete behavioral signals. The architecture resolves the uncertainty of sparse observational data through abductive Counterfactual Simulation (injecting unobserved hypothetical phenomena to infer hidden causal links). By executing these algorithms on a formally closed substrate governed by the invariant-preserving algebra of Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC), we establish a theoretical framework for an autonomous reasoning engine designed to enforce logical auditability and structurally constrain the propagation of weak logical steps.

title:
Your Loss is My Gain: 
Low Stake Attacks on Liquid Staking Pools
affiliations: Yale University, Yale University, Imperial College London - Department of Computing and Yale University

detail.title:
Your Loss is My Gain: 
Low Stake Attacks on Liquid Staking Pools
detail.abstract:
Permissionless Proof-of-Stake (PoS) economic security is predicated on the high cost of violating consensus safety or liveness. We show that liquid staking introduces additional risks that are not captured by standard PoS economic security arguments. Through an empirical study of Ethereum data, we find that the operational performance of liquid staking pools is positively associated with subsequent normalized liquid staking token (LST) returns. Motivated by this, we present a cross-layer attack: a low-stake adversary can manipulate the consensus protocol to degrade a target pool's performance and take application-layer positions that profit if the market reprices the corresponding liquid staking token (LST) in-line with the historically observed association. 
     To make the consensus layer manipulation concrete, we develop a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework to automatically discover attack strategies. Our evaluation shows that the learned strategies can recover near-optimal theoretical attacks and uncover new manipulation behaviors that significantly degrade target pool performance. We further characterize feasible application-layer monetization channels and analyze leveraged shorting in detail using Monte Carlo simulations, showing that such attacks can be profitable with over one-half probability for LSTs of major staking pools. Our findings reveal a previously overlooked attack surface in PoS systems with liquid staking and expose a gap between consensus and economic security.

title: Individual Risk-Taking and Its Effects on Family Dynamics
affiliations: Obra D Tompkins High School

detail.title: Individual Risk-Taking and Its Effects on Family Dynamics
detail.abstract: The purpose of this research is to understand the effects an individual’s risk-taking behaviors have on the dynamics of the intermediate family. Prior research emphasized some psychological factors that affect the family in a household with an individual who takes financial risks. talk about different factors that affect the family such as the household environment, situational, and existing mental health. However, there was limited research on the long-term financial effects within a risk-taking household and the standard of living of non-risking taking individuals, this is the gap I aim to explore. To collect my data, I conducted interviews where I used separate sets of questions for the participants that took risks and their family members. The individual was asked about their income, financial background, and financial environment as they matured. On the other hand, the family members were asked about their relationship with the individual, their financial environment, and their ideas about finances. This way, I was able to find correlations between the individuals financial habits and how their families respond to them. For example, I found a correlation between money habits and the participants salary, and how the family members reacted to these habits. From this, I concluded that the amount of risk-taking an individual takes greatly affects their family. It shapes how their family views financial matters, and there is positive growth when a family is open about their finances in the home. This positive growth in financial decision making, due to open discussion of finances, allows people to start off with a good financial literacy early in life, compared to people who didn’t receive the knowledge who start later. And finally, risk-taking heavily depends on the income an individual makes. Individuals with higher salaries may be more likely to take financial risks, while those with a lower salary may be less likely to take those risks. Future INDIVIDUAL RISK-TAKING AND ITS EFFECTS ON FAMILY DYNAMICS 3 research should include the psychological effects that play a role in these processes and also include more participants in order to obtain more consistent data.

title: Private Equity and Venture Capital in Institutional Portfolios: From Asset-Class Labels to Exposure-Based Allocation

detail.title: Private Equity and Venture Capital in Institutional Portfolios: From Asset-Class Labels to Exposure-Based Allocation
detail.abstract:
Private equity and venture capital are widely treated as asset classes within institutional portfolios, providing a convenient framework for allocation, reporting, and benchmarking. However, this classification masks substantial variation in underlying exposures, liquidity characteristics, and governance requirements across strategies. While institutional investors are generally aware of this heterogeneity, allocation and evaluation frameworks continue to rely on simplified labels, creating a persistent gap between how capital is categorized and how it behaves in practice.

This paper examines whether private equity and venture capital function as coherent asset classes, or whether they are better understood as implementation channels through which distinct exposures are accessed. By analyzing risk, return dispersion, liquidity constraints, and governance demands, the paper shows that outcomes in private markets are driven less by the asset-class label and more by strategy selection, manager access, and institutional capability.

Reframing private equity and venture capital as implementation channels provides a more precise foundation for portfolio design. It shifts the focus from category-based allocation toward exposure-based decision-making, improving alignment between investment objectives, portfolio construction, and realized outcomes. The paper concludes that while asset-class labels remain useful for communication and governance, effective institutional investing requires a more explicit understanding of the exposures they represent.

detail.abstract: Classical economics defines three functions of money-medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value-all from the perspective of exchange. Each answers the question: what does money do? This paper proposes a fourth function: money as a generalized social access right to resources detached from physical possession. It answers a different question: what does money allow economic agents not to do?-namely, to hold all physical resources necessary for survival. Using the warehouse analogy-the market as a social warehouse, money as the withdrawal voucherthe paper demonstrates why the classical three functions leave a deeper anthropological layer

title: Recalibrating the Country Risk Premium in a Fractured Global Economy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Recalibrating the Country Risk Premium in a Fractured Global Economy
detail.abstract:
Corporate finance is currently mispricing trillions of dollars in global capital by relying on an obsolete assumption: the existence of a seamlessly integrated, borderless economy. As global supply chains weaponize and nations aggressively transition into state-managed Fortress Economies, traditional valuation frameworks anchored by the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) and orthodox Country Risk Premiums (CRP) are experiencing a catastrophic structural failure.

This paper demonstrates that orthodox CRP methodologies, which rely on historical relative equity volatility, suffer from a Volatility Paradox. In state-managed economies, aggressive sovereign interventions such as capital controls, short-selling bans, and Sovereign Wealth Fund deployments artificially compress domestic equity variance. Consequently, traditional valuation models mechanically collapse, shrinking discount rates and artificially subsidizing the cost of capital precisely when systemic geopolitical risk is most acute.

To rectify this systemic mispricing, this study introduces the Geopolitical Risk Premium (GRP) framework. The GRP anchors baseline risk to offshore Sovereign Credit Default Swap (CDS) spreads, bypassing onshore financial repression. It dynamically scales this baseline via a novel Risk Multiplier that synthesizes physical vulnerability utilizing Automatic Identification System (AIS) maritime choke point data against a nation’s macroeconomic absorptive capacity, termed Fortress Insulation. Furthermore, the paper replaces traditional geographic revenue metrics with a multi-factor Adjusted Lambda, which explicitly disaggregates firm-specific risk into physical supply chain reliance and state-sponsored protection.

Through rigorous empirical case studies of insulated regional powers (India’s infrastructure monopolies), vulnerable integrated exporters (Germany’s automotive sector), and forcibly closed-loop economies (Russia and Iran), this research proves that geographic financial domicile is a dangerously obsolete proxy for corporate risk. Ultimately, the findings mandate a paradigm shift in capital allocation, urging practitioners to abandon deterministic discount rates in favor of probabilistic, scenario-based Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) models that explicitly price geopolitical friction directly into micro-level cash flows.

title: Government’s economic management and citizen satisfaction: a Partisan Disconfirmation Model
affiliations: Stellenbosch University and University of Cape Town

detail.title: Government’s economic management and citizen satisfaction: a Partisan Disconfirmation Model

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable

detail.abstract:
Introduction: How do citizens evaluate government economic performance? Although both economic perceptions and partisan identity are known to shape political attitudes, their interaction remains poorly understood. This study develops a Partisan Disconfirmation Model (PDM), integrating expectancy–disconfirmation theory (EDT) with partisan identity to explain how citizens form satisfaction judgments about government economic management.

Methods: The study uses a nationally representative Afrobarometer survey data from Malawi (N = 1,200). Ordered logistic regression models are estimated to examine how perceptions of national economic conditions and partisan identification influence satisfaction with government economic management. The analysis includes interaction terms to assess whether partisan effects vary across economic contexts. Hypotheses are evaluated using omnibus Wald tests of joint parameter significance, alongside post-estimation contrasts based on predicted probabilities.

Results: Perceived economic performance emerges as the strongest predictor of satisfaction, with more positive evaluations significantly increasing the likelihood of favourable assessments of government economic management. Partisan alignment also shapes evaluations, as ruling-party identifiers report higher satisfaction than opposition supporters. While joint tests confirm the independent effects of economic perceptions and partisanship, post-estimation contrasts provide no evidence that partisan effects vary across economic contexts, indicating that these influences operate independently rather than conditionally.

Discussion: The findings highlight the central role of economic performance perceptions in shaping satisfaction with government economic management. Although partisanship influences baseline attitudes, the absence of conditional partisan belief updating suggests that economic perceptions and partisan identity exert independent effects, rather than interacting through a disconfirmation process as predicted by the PDM.

title: Just Transition in Québec
affiliations: l’École des relations Industrielles, Université de Montréal, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Quebec at Montreal (UQAM) - Université du Québec à Montréal

detail.title: Just Transition in Québec

declarations.funderStatement: This report was produced as part of the Hans-Böckler-Foundation funded project “Just Transition: Aktivitäten im internationalen Vergleich”. The project focuses on studying Just Transitions by comparing concepts, policies, and strategies across 14 diverse countries to ensure a socially just shift towards decarbonisation. It aims to develop recommendations for climate- friendly structural changes that protect workers and vulnerable groups. The project is funded by the Hans Böckler Foundation – Just Transition: Aktivitäten im internationalen Vergleich 2021-582-2.

detail.abstract: This report focuses on engagement by Trade Unions in the province of Québec, Canada on climate change issues and how more generally they contribute to Just Transition. By exploring the structure of labour and climate policies, we seek to identify the levers available to unions in the fight against climate change. In doing so, we highlight the tensions that exist within the industrial relations system and within union organizations around just transition issues. In Québec, trade unions made the shift towards just transition in the years leading up to the Paris Agreement and have since taken up its definition. They were critical players in the coalitions that led to the social consensus in Québec’s for a strong decarbonization trajectory. These coalitions were created in the wake of environmental conflicts around fossil fuel extractive infrastructure projects between 2010 and 2021 when Québec passed a law banning the future extraction of oil and gas on its territory and cancelling any existing licences or permits to explore and extract. Union participation in these coalitions was instrumental to their success. Today, the main challenges in implementing decarbonisation are centred on the electrification of industry and transport, which means that workers will have to adapt to new technical processes and new technologies. The transition is therefore essentially driven by issues relating to the training of workers, the match between training and employment and the search for investment to guarantee jobs.

title: BORDERLESS COMMERCE, TERRITORIAL RIGHTS: REASSESSING TRIPS IN THE AGE OF E-COMMERCE

detail.title: BORDERLESS COMMERCE, TERRITORIAL RIGHTS: REASSESSING TRIPS IN THE AGE OF E-COMMERCE
detail.abstract: The Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) was negotiated in 1994, before the commercial internet had meaningfully emerged as a global economic system. Amazon had not yet been founded. The World Wide Web remained limited in scale, and electronic commerce occupied little space in multilateral trade discussions. Yet the same agreement now governs the intellectual property dimensions of a digital economy worth trillions of dollars, where software, databases, copyrighted works, trademarks, and patented technologies move across borders almost instantaneously through networks the agreement's drafters could scarcely have anticipated. The WTO's 1998 Work Programme on Electronic Commerce reflected an early recognition that the existing multilateral framework was beginning to encounter problems it had not been designed to address. The 1999 TRIPS Council Report identified several of them directly: online copyright infringement, the territorial nature of intellectual property rights, uncertainty over jurisdiction, and the unresolved classification of electronically transmitted products. More than twenty-five years later, many of those same questions continue to shape debates within international trade law. This paper argues that the principal difficulty is not the absence of intellectual property protection under TRIPS. In many respects, the agreement continues to provide an important legal foundation for copyright, patent, and trademark protection in the digital environment. A legal setup based on territorial enforcement mechanisms struggles to regulate commercial activity that occurs simultaneously across multiple jurisdictions through borderless digital networks. The discussion traces this issue across copyright, patent, trademark, geographical indication, and enforcement frameworks. It also examines the institutional response within the WTO system, including the July 2024 Joint Statement Initiative on Electronic Commerce, and considers the extent to which these developments have addressed the underlying difficulties. The paper concludes that, despite important institutional efforts, many of the structural issues identified during the early development of electronic commerce remain substantially unresolved.

title: Reconstructing Identity Through Narrative Voice Language, Memory, and Structures of Power in Contemporary English Literature
affiliations: P P Savani University, P P Savani University, P P Savani University, P P Savani University, DR G R D College of Science and Chandigarh University

detail.title: Reconstructing Identity Through Narrative Voice Language, Memory, and Structures of Power in Contemporary English Literature

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Reconstructing Identity Through Narrative Voice Language, Memory, and Structures of Power in Contemporary English Literature
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: The contemporary English literature is increasingly becoming involved in the reconstruction of identity through narrative voice, representation of language, and politics of memory. Identity in the context of modern literature is no longer addressed as a fixed or stable concept but as a fluid construction that is mediated by language, recollection of the past and sociopolitical configurations people are placed in as subjective agents. Narrative voice is a useful resource that can help to negotiate the subjectivity of characters by offering the personal past and cultural belonging and power structures. The paper will address how narrative voice is used in contemporary literary works to reconstruct the identity by utilizing language to express themselves and build discourses of memory and power relations in social institutions such as colonial history, gendering relations and cultural authority. Interdisciplinary theoretical approaches of postcolonial theory, narratology, memory studies, and critical discourse analysis underlie the study to investigate how literary language is a medium through which the voices of the oppressed are expressed as a resistance and a way to define themselves. The textual analysis research approach the paper adheres to is a qualitative approach that is sensitive to the chosen contemporary English novels that dwell upon the migration, postcolonial identity, gender politics and cultural memory. The study also determines the narrative techniques replicated in close reading/discourse analysis like fragmented narration, unreliable narrators, shifting perspectives, and linguistic hybridity. These approaches help authors to describe identity as the process, which is dynamic and forced by the process of memory reconstruction and bargaining of power. The findings suggest that narrative voice is not simply a storytelling instrument but a political/cultural instrument whereby the individuals reclaim their ability in the systems of oppression. Moreover, as seen in the discussion, memory narratives are known to discredit the mainstream narratives of the past since they create an alternative history that foreshadows the marginal experiences. Putting narrative voice at the intersection area of cross-cultural engagement between the language, memory, and power, the study contributes to the existing literature research by demonstrating how fiction can play a role in the broader social cultural discourse on identity formation in the globalized world. The paper determines the importance of narrative representation to the act of forming collective memory and cultural identity, where literature is a good place where critical space can be found where an individual and a community can renegotiate their relationship to history, power, and self..

detail.abstract: The overall objectives of the study were to identify the major forms of human disturbance in the Cumilla Sal forests; to assess the effects of disturbance on biodiversity and forest structure; and to recommend conservation and sustainable management strategies. The study revealed that Shorea robusta was the primary tree species in the fragmented remnants, accompanied by Careya arborea, Bauhinia spp., and Holarrhena pubescens. The family Leguminosae was the highest in species count, followed by Euphorbiaceae and Rubiaceae. Moving away from top-down bureaucratic approaches toward more people-centric models is highly warranted.

title: From AI Governance Structures to Risk Exposure Regimes: A Configurational Model of Organisational Vulnerability

detail.title: From AI Governance Structures to Risk Exposure Regimes: A Configurational Model of Organisational Vulnerability
detail.abstract: Despite increasing awareness of the risks associated with artificial intelligence (AI), there is limited understanding of how organisational governance structures affect firms' exposure to these risks. Current research and policy often focus on ethical principles and technical measures, assuming that organisations can implement effective governance. This paper challenges that assumption, arguing that governance design plays a more critical role in determining AI-related risk than technological complexity. Based on earlier empirical research involving 351 organisations, the study finds that AI governance roles are unevenly distributed, poorly integrated, and often lack the authority and resources needed for effective oversight. It introduces a model that connects governance structure, defined by authority, resource allocation, and organisational integration, to firm-level risk. The paper categorises four governance configurations: Governance Absence, Symbolic Governance, Operational Governance, and Institutionalised Governance, highlighting their different impacts on risk visibility, controllability, and accountability. Additionally, it identifies three mechanisms-decision risk, monitoring failure, and accountability fragmentation-through which governance misalignments lead to organisational vulnerability. The results indicate that having governance roles does not necessarily mitigate risk. For example, symbolic governance can create mispriced risk when perceived control is high. By framing AI risk as a function of organisational design, this paper advances discussions on AI governance, organisational theory, and risk management by introducing a configurational perspective on organisational vulnerability. The paper is conceptual but empirically anchored in cross-sectoral evidence on governance structures.

title: Upstream Disclosure, Downstream Assurance: EHDS Article 78 as a Compliance Pathway for AI Act Article 10 in Medical AI
affiliations: University of Copenhagen - Centre for Advanced Studies in Bioscience Innovation Law (CeBIL), University of Copenhagen - Centre for Advanced Studies in Bioscience Innovation Law (CeBIL) and LML, University of Cambridge

detail.title: Upstream Disclosure, Downstream Assurance: EHDS Article 78 as a Compliance Pathway for AI Act Article 10 in Medical AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: This work was made possible through the generous support of the Novo Nordisk Foundation (NNF) via a grant for the scientifically independent Collaborative Research Program in Bioscience Innovation Law (Inter-CeBIL Program – Grant No. NNF23SA0087056).

detail.abstract: The EU AI Act (AIA) and the European Health Data Space Regulation (EHDS) will progressively shape data governance for medical AI systems in Europe. Article 10 AIA requires providers of highrisk AI systems to use datasets that are representative, bias-examined, and documented. Article 78 EHDS establishes a data quality and utility label whose technical specifications, to be adopted by March 2027, must be designed with regard to Article 10 AIA requirements. This paper analyses the relationship between these provisions, distinguishing between upstream disclosure (of the quality and utility of information produced by health data holders) and downstream assurance (of AI systemspecific data quality and governance). Using the example of a diagnostic radiology AI system, this paper finds that the Article 78 EHDS label can serve as meaningful compliance evidence for Article 10 AIA requirements that are dataset-level in character, particularly concerning documentation of data origins, technical quality, and population representativity. For obligations that depend on the AI system's intended purpose, deployment context, or model architecture, the label informs, but cannot discharge, the provider's responsibility. Several tensions between the two instruments constrain the pathway further, including EHDS preference for pseudonymisation and anonymisation as early as possible, the narrow and legally uncertain GDPR gateway for commercial providers seeking pseudonymised data for bias detection, the timeline gap between the instruments' respective application dates, and incentive gaps on each side of the labelling framework. The proposed Digital Omnibus reforms, currently in legislative flux, do not resolve the GDPR difficulty for commercial providers. The regulatory bridge created by Article 78(6) EHDS may meaningfully reduce compliance burdens and improve the evidentiary basis for bias examination, but only where the implementing acts operationalise the cross-reference in a substantive manner. The bridge is, therefore, narrower than its text alone might suggest, and complementary implementation measures will be needed if EHDSlabelled data is to serve as a practical compliance resource for medical AI providers.

title: Interpretations of Stakeholder Theory: Economic, Philosophical and Political
affiliations: George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School

detail.title: Interpretations of Stakeholder Theory: Economic, Philosophical and Political
detail.abstract: In contrast to Delaware law, which requires that directors manage the corporation for the benefit of its shareholders, stakeholder theory holds that directors should manage the corporation for the benefit of all those affected by its operations. Historically, the class of stakeholders has included, besides shareholders, such corporate constituencies as employees, customers, creditors, suppliers, and the communities in which the corporation operates; nowadays, a concern for climate change can expand the class of stakeholders to include all human beings now living or to be born in the future. The central problem with stakeholder theory, acknowledged even by some of its leading advocates, is that saying directors should take account of the interests of all stakeholders does nothing to determine which interests of which affected individuals are cognizable and which are not, much less how benefits to some stakeholders should be traded off against harms to others. This article suggests that there are three main ways to provide stakeholder theory with the needed normative content to answer such questions: (a) a welfare economic approach, which assumes that the preferences of individual stakeholders should determine what is best for all stakeholders collectively and which thus makes stakeholder theory into an exercise in welfare economics, (b) a moral philosophical approach, which supplements stakeholder theory with any of various moral philosophies (such as a Rawlsian theory of justice or a Thomistic natural law theory) to guide the directors’ business decisions, or (c) a political approach, in which the corporate franchise is extended to all or most stakeholders, thus presumably making directors responsive to the concerns of such stakeholders and converting business decisions into political compromises among various constituencies. The article argues that none of these approaches is likely to result in a viable theory of corporate governance.

title: Dynamic Prediction of Waiting Time Intervals: Application to Cancer Care Facilities
affiliations: , University of Toronto and University of Rochester - Simon Business School

detail.title: Dynamic Prediction of Waiting Time Intervals: Application to Cancer Care Facilities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: One of the authors worked as a summer intern for the company on the project.

detail.abstract:
We study the problem of predicting in real-time customers' waiting time. We focus on (1) service systems where customers are scheduled for service ahead of time and where real-time and scheduling data is available to the model (e.g., in cancer care); and (2) the predictions are intervals that are dynamically updated over time (a format supported by practice and research). We collaborate with a large cancer hospital and conduct an extensive set of numerical experiments using recent operational data. We compare a broad set of methodologies and report on their performance in terms of interval width and accuracy, two contrasting yet desirable objectives. We further develop and evaluate a prototype in a preliminary field experiment. 
Our study shows that Random Survival Forest outperforms other Machine Learning models, establishing itself as state-of-the-art. We find that despite the availability of a rich dataset, creating accurate predictive models is challenging due to stochasticity, heterogeneity, the complex service process, and limitations of the available data. A simulation study suggests that the quality of prediction could not be improved due to an irreducible error. Our experiments also show that while real time data substantially improves the prediction quality, hospitals can still benefit from such models without investing in infrastructure that supports real time tracking of patients and providers. Finally, we discuss lessons learned from the development process, including the customization of predictive models to improve performance and usability, the use of Explainable AI, and ways in which future endeavors could potentially create better models.

title: Labor Mobility Restrictions and Exploratory Innovation: Evidence from the Inevitable Disclosure Doctrine
affiliations: Wilfrid Laurier University - Lazaridis School of Business & Economics

detail.title: Labor Mobility Restrictions and Exploratory Innovation: Evidence from the Inevitable Disclosure Doctrine

declarations.funderStatement: I acknowledge financial support from the Lazaridis Institute and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (Grant Number: 435-2024-0363).

detail.abstract: We examine how legal restrictions on inventor mobility shape the composition of corporate innovation. Exploiting the staggered adoption of the Inevitable Disclosure Doctrine by U.S. state courts between 1980 and 2021, we find that affected firms reweight their patent portfolios toward exploratory research in new technological domains and away from exploitative refinements of their existing knowledge base. The compositional shift is supported by direct evidence on the underlying labor-mobility mechanism: following adoption, fewer of a firm's inventors depart for technologically related peer firms. Consistent with this retention effect, firms accumulate a larger share of star inventors and produce patents of substantially higher citation impact, even as raw patent counts decline. The reweighting is most pronounced among firms with limited exposure to technology spillovers, concentrated inventor bases, or operations in technologically thinner fields, where the protection of internally accumulated tacit knowledge is most valuable. Our findings identify a previously underappreciated benefit of restrictions on inventor mobility, namely their role in fostering long-horizon, high-impact innovation.

title: JURISDICTION AND CHOICE OF LAW IN DISPUTES RELATING TO CROSS-BORDER NFT TRANSACTIONS: THE CASE FOR UNIFORM PRIVATE INTERNATIONAL LAW RULES
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: JURISDICTION AND CHOICE OF LAW IN DISPUTES RELATING TO CROSS-BORDER NFT TRANSACTIONS: THE CASE FOR UNIFORM PRIVATE INTERNATIONAL LAW RULES
detail.abstract:
The recent collapse of large crypto exchanges like FTX has drawn much public attention to the cryptoasset space. Despite the decline of cryptocurrencies, non-fungible tokens (NFTs), another type of cryptoasset, have risen in popularity with about $946 million in trading volume in January 2023. A common feature of NFTs and cryptocurrencies is that they are both applications of blockchain technology. While some proponents have argued that the law is irrelevant to the blockchain, this article argues that law is relevant because blockchain technology does not provide a remedy for all cases that may arise from its use. Furthermore, blockchain technology cannot determine the validity or legality of NFT and cryptocurrency smart contracts under national laws, and courts in litigation will need to determine which law governs these questions. Blockchain-based smart contracts (including NFTs) will, as this article argues, have a foreign element because the blockchain nodes are in various jurisdictions, as are, often, the parties to the contracts. It is therefore vital to understand how conflict of law rules determine the jurisdiction and applicable law in NFT-related disputes.

This article offers the first comprehensive examination of the issues of jurisdiction and choice of law that arise in NFT-related disputes. It analyzes the major extant private international law frameworks, including the Brussels I (recast) Regulation, the CISG, and the Rome I & II Regulations, and shows why they are inadequate for addressing these issues, largely because the concepts in these frameworks do not easily apply to the features of the blockchain that arise in NFT-related disputes. This article also examines UK jurisprudence on cryptoassets and NFT-related case law across various jurisdictions and the potential of the UNIDROIT Principles on Digital Assets and Private Law, which address blockchain issues better than other frameworks. Furthermore, the article examines all pertinent case law on these questions.

The article makes a number of contributions. It explains in detail the various factors that are important for a successful application of the traditional private international law rules to NFT-related disputes, and it demonstrates the challenges of applying traditional choice of law rules in this area. These challenges, the article shows, are even more complex for NFT-related disputes than for seemingly analogous disputes that have arisen in the context of cross-border Internet transactions. The article also analyzes the main alternatives to national choice of law, including lex cryptographia, uniform substantive law rules, and uniform private international law rules. The article concludes that developing uniform private international law rules for NFT-related disputes is the most feasible and efficient solution that has a better chance of acceptability and workability than the other proposals.

This article proceeds as follows: Part I describes the relevance of law to the blockchain. Part II defines the technological concepts that are relevant to the legal analysis. Part III discusses the jurisdiction issues that arise in disputes relating to NFT transactions. Part IV discusses choice of law issues. Part V makes an argument about how to resolve these issues.

title: Living Large? Housing Consumption and Income Growth
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Department of Economics, Students

detail.title: Living Large? Housing Consumption and Income Growth
detail.abstract: This paper documents the upward trend in American housing consumption and quantifies the corresponding role of income growth. I estimate income elasticities of household-level demand of 0.2 for housing size and 0.4 for home value, highlighting the importance of disentangling quantity responses from amenities. Interacting a shift share instrument with contemporary zoning measures, I find that rising incomes inflate house prices but have recently spurred relative declines in home sizes. To investigate the divergence between household-and market-level responses, I estimate a quantitative model of local housing market equilibrium, allowing for counterfactual computations. Had housing supply remained elastic, realized income growth would have increased home sizes between 1.6% and 3.2%, demonstrating that housing regulation suppresses quantity gains to income, despite housing being a normal good. Further, more elastic housing demand can be credited with up to one-quarter of recent house price responses to income. These findings reveal that accounting for households' substantial income elasticity of housing size is critical to understanding market dynamics.

title: Extrapolative Commodity Returns
affiliations: , Zhejiang University - School of Economics and Academy of Financial Research and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance (SAIF)

detail.title: Extrapolative Commodity Returns
detail.abstract: We investigate the role of extrapolation in commodity markets. Non-commercial traders exhibit extrapolative beliefs while commercial traders do not. We construct a novel holding-based commodity measure of the degree of extrapolation (DOX). DOX positively predicts the cross-section of commodity returns. The predictive power cannot be explained by existing risk factors or characteristics. The predictability is consistent with the liquidity provision due to gradual unwinding of extrapolators and limits to arbitrage. Investors even extrapolate the term structure. We further offer an extrapolation-based interpretation for commodity momentum and value. An extrapolation-augmented factor model explains commodity anomalies and individual commodity returns well.

title: Countdown to the close: Order dynamics in the pre-auction phase at the close on the LSE
affiliations: University of Melbourne - Department of Finance and

detail.title: Countdown to the close: Order dynamics in the pre-auction phase at the close on the LSE
detail.abstract: This paper examines order submission and price formation during the London Stock Exchange closing pre-auction for FTSE 100 stocks. We document strategic timing: activity clusters at the opening and final minute, peaking about 30 seconds before uncrossing. Traders rely predominantly on limit orders, prioritising price control over execution certainty, while market order use rises on index rebalancing days when execution urgency is greatest. Rebalance days exhibit higher volumes, larger and more persistent imbalances, and more volatile indicative prices that converge more slowly to final auction prices. Overall, the auction design appears to support orderly price formation through transparency and randomised timing

title: To Wait or to Wed? The Effect of Gold Price Fluctuations on Decisions on the Timing of Marriage
affiliations: , University of Maine and Texas A&M University

detail.title: To Wait or to Wed? The Effect of Gold Price Fluctuations on Decisions on the Timing of Marriage
detail.abstract: We examine the effect of gold price fluctuations on decisions regarding the timing of marriage in China, where gold plays an essential role in wedding customs. Using Chinese provincial-level panel data from 2006 to 2023 and an instrument based on monetary policy uncertainty, we find that higher growth in gold prices significantly increases the growth rate of first-time marriages, indicating that anticipated future increases in marriage-related costs can induce earlier marriage timing and suggesting the ‘price expectation effect’. The findings suggest that couples accelerate marriage timing in response to rising gold prices, highlighting an innovative channel through which financial markets influence aggregate demographic behaviour.

title: Tribal Comanagement at the State Level: The Oregon Experience
affiliations: Lewis & Clark College - Lewis & Clark Law School and Lewis & Clark College - Lewis & Clark Law School

detail.title: Tribal Comanagement at the State Level: The Oregon Experience
detail.abstract: Ecological disturbances are straining conventional fish and wildlife management, which tribal knowledge can inform to produce more effective management. Although federal policy has recognized government-to-government relations with Tribal Nations, most day-today regulation of fish and wildlife runs through state agencies. This Article argues that Oregon has provided an important management framework between the state and Tribal Nations. Since 2022, Oregon has entered a series of state-tribal agreements that constitute a durable and increasingly replicable co-management framework. This Article contends that these agreements reflect a second-generation, state-driven adaptation of an earlier co-management framework that emerged from the Columbia River treaty-rights litigation. Although Oregon has not formally ceded legal primacy, the agreements nonetheless shift considerable operational authority to Tribal Nations through recurring harvest negotiation, shared scientific information, hunting and fishing licensing, and habitat coordination. Some limits to the co-management framework appear in Willamette Falls, an important historic intertribal commons, where overlapping tribal claims expose the shortcomings of bilateralism. Habitat restoration likewise tests whether Oregon's framework can apply beyond the harvest context. Consequently, the Article concludes that the Oregon-tribal agreements offer a workable but conditional framework of inter-sovereign resource management for other states and Tribal Nations, and other resources.

title: ANATOMY OF THE RETEST IN THE QQQ OPENING RANGE BREAKOUT
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: ANATOMY OF THE RETEST IN THE QQQ OPENING RANGE BREAKOUT

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently with no financial relationships with any organization that could influence the results.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper is an exploratory and descriptive study. The author makes no claims of causality or exploitability regarding the documented patterns. We present an exploratory study of the post-breakout sequence in the Invesco QQQ Trust ETF, using intraday data at one-minute resolution from January 2017 through December 2024. The existing literature on the Opening Range Breakout focuses on entry at the moment of the breakout; the internal dynamics of the minutes that follow have not been measured to date. We decompose the sequence into four levels-the opening range, the breakout, the retest, and the outcome-and document the statistical associations observed at each level. We find that range size is associated with the magnitude of the subsequent move, that a consistent fraction of breakouts generates a retest of the broken level within a defined time window, that the time elapsed until that retest shows the strongest association with the subsequent outcome, and that larger pre-retest excursions are associated with a lower probability of continuation-a counterintuitive pattern that we document along with its interpretive limitations. All results are descriptive associations conditional on operational definitions that we document with precision. Causal mechanisms are unknown. We invite other researchers to replicate, challenge, and extend this work.

title: The Rise and Fall of the Mongol Empire
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Rise and Fall of the Mongol Empire
detail.abstract:
This paper is an undergraduate economic history research study examining the rise, expansion, and decline of the Mongol Empire expansion. It analyzes how Mongol military innovation, institutional structures, and trade policies contributed to the creation of one of the largest contiguous empires in history and facilitated unprecedented economic integration across Eurasia. Particular attention is given to the role of the Silk Road, merchant networks, taxation systems, and state-supported trade infrastructure in promoting interregional exchange.

The study also evaluates the economic consequences of Mongol governance, including reliance on merchant intermediaries, fiscal policies under Ögedei Khan, and the expansion of credit and taxation systems. While the empire initially enhanced trade efficiency and cultural exchange, excessive state expenditures, decentralized merchant influence, and fiscal imbalances contributed to long-term instability. The paper argues that the Mongol Empire provides an early historical case study of large-scale economic integration accompanied by structural vulnerabilities arising from rapid expansion and institutional overreach.

Overall, this research highlights the importance of trade institutions, fiscal management, and governance structures in sustaining long-run economic stability, offering insights relevant to both historical and modern economic systems.
