title: UNDERSTANDING CORPORATE PURPOSE & ETHICS
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: UNDERSTANDING CORPORATE PURPOSE & ETHICS

publicationDetails.detailsText: CERDEL Multidisciplinary Journal of African Development, 3(1), 168–184. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20129152

detail.abstract: The focus is on highlighting the alignment of purpose with strategy, ethics, and governance to foster long-term sustainability and legitimacy. The paper posit that understanding corporate purpose and ethics should synthesize the shift from shareholder primacy to a broader stakeholder model, emphasizing that profit is derived from solving problems, not creating them. Consequently, it portends understanding corporate purpose in the modern context demands a reevaluation of business goals, moving beyond profit maximization to embrace ethical accountability and stakeholder value. Therefore, it duels on how embedding ethical principles-fairness, transparency, and responsibility-into corporate strategy, strengthens reputation and long-term sustainability. In addition, it explores the imperative to connect corporate purpose with day-today operations and governance structures to ensure that company solves societal problems without creating harm.

title: When Does Generative AI Improve Innovation Efficiency? Organisational Culture as a Complementary Capability
affiliations: University of Birmingham and University of Westminster

detail.title: When Does Generative AI Improve Innovation Efficiency? Organisational Culture as a Complementary Capability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A

detail.abstract: The release of ChatGPT represents one of the most significant recent shocks to the way organisations and individuals work, as generative AI became rapidly accessible beyond specialised technical settings. This shift may have substantial implications for productivity and innovation, particularly for how firms convert R&D investment into revenue and growth. However, these effects are unlikely to be uniform across firms. This paper examines whether organisational culture acts as a complementary capability that moderates the effect of generative AI exposure on firm-level innovation efficiency. Using the public release of ChatGPT in November 2022 as a technological shock, we document a decline in innovation efficiency among US research-intensive public firms after the release. We further show that this decline is less pronounced among firms with stronger innovation-and adaptability-oriented cultures. These findings suggest that the innovation effects of generative AI depend not only on technological exposure, but also on firms' organisational capacity to adapt, experiment and integrate new tools into existing R&D routines.

title: Governed Intelligence Architecture for Institutional AI
affiliations: Capgemini and Capgemini

detail.title: Governed Intelligence Architecture for Institutional AI
detail.abstract:
AI adoption has outpaced the epistemic infrastructure required to make institutional AI reliable. In regulated organizations, AI systems do not act on knowledge in the abstract — they act on claims whose provenance, scope, freshness, coherence, and authority determine whether outputs are usable, auditable, and safe. This paper introduces epistemic immunity: a governed defense architecture for protecting institutional knowledge substrates from six systemic failure modes — pollution, staleness, fragmentation, amnesia, cascade failure, and structural distortion.
The paper distinguishes knowledge from intelligence. Knowledge is validated, contextual, and relational understanding distributed across people, systems, records, and practices. Intelligence is the governed capacity to mobilize that knowledge into reliable judgment and action under changing conditions. Governed intelligence therefore requires more than AI capability: it requires knowledge infrastructure that can admit, validate, scope, demote, preserve, and renew claims over time.
Epistemic immunity is operationalized through the Governed Intelligence Lifecycle — Ingest, Consolidate, Curate, Expand, and Apply — and specified through a three-scope capability architecture covering claim-level controls, graph-level integrity, and delivery-level access, explanation, and agent action. The framework draws on distributed cognition, sensemaking, autopoiesis, dissipative structures, and the adjacent possible to argue that institutional knowledge is not a static asset but a continuously regenerated socio-technical system.
Applied to financial services, the paper shows how regulated institutions can move beyond retrieval-oriented AI toward governed intelligence systems that preserve provenance, manage decay, surface contradictions, constrain agent action, and compound learning without accumulating epistemic debt. The paper develops a conceptual architecture grounded in distributed cognition and knowledge governance traditions, operationalized as an implementation methodology, and applied to the regulatory and operational context of financial services.
This is Paper D of a five-paper programme: Paper A (Reichhart and Gelas, 2026a) diagnoses dynamics blindness as the failure mechanism; Paper B (Gelas and Reichhart, 2026b) specifies the architectural resolution — a tripartite structure of state, dynamics, and agency layers; Paper C (Reichhart and Gelas, 2026c) provides theoretical foundations from ten independent traditions; this paper operationalizes the methodology; Paper E (Reichhart and Gelas, 2026e) identifies the conditions under which the architecture produces governed initiative rather than mere autonomy.

title:
STRUCTURAL DECISIONS IN ACCELERATED SYSTEMS:

Institutional Reflections on Coordination, Continuity and Accountability

detail.title:
STRUCTURAL DECISIONS IN ACCELERATED SYSTEMS:

Institutional Reflections on Coordination, Continuity and Accountability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I confirm research integrity for this paper
declarations.ethicsApproval: This publication is a conceptual institutional reflection based on publicly available historical, policy and institutional information sources. The work does not involve human participants, clinical experimentation, confidential institutional data or identifiable personal information. Formal ethics committee approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: The author declares no commercial conflict of interest directly associated with the publication of this paper.

detail.abstract:
Institutions across finance, infrastructure, technology, public administration and global governance increasingly operate within environments defined by acceleration, interdependence and systemic coordination pressure. As operational systems become more interconnected, continuity risks may emerge not only from isolated institutional failures, but from structural gaps between rapidly evolving technological environments and slower-moving coordination architectures.

This paper presents a series of institutional reflections informed by historical precedent, infrastructure interdependence and recurring structural patterns observed across periods of technological, economic and geopolitical transition. The objective is not predictive certainty, but strategic interpretation: examining how continuity pressures, coordination constraints and accountability challenges may increasingly shape institutional resilience within accelerated operational systems.

The paper explores nine emerging structural pressures, each paired with historical parallels and broader institutional continuity considerations. Across these reflections, a recurring theme emerges: many institutional disruptions historically evolved not from informational absence, but from delayed coordination, fragmented adaptation and reactive governance development after continuity pressures had already intensified.

The paper concludes by proposing that institutional resilience in accelerated systems may increasingly depend on earlier coordination capacity, stronger continuity visibility and more adaptive accountability structures capable of evolving alongside increasingly interconnected operational environments.

title: Generative AI and Firm-Candidate Dynamics in the Labor Market
affiliations: , Fudan University - School of Management and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Generative AI and Firm-Candidate Dynamics in the Labor Market
detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is significantly reshaping the labor market. While existing literature primarily focuses on GenAI's isolated effects on either labor demand (e.g., task automation) or labor supply (e.g., skill development), research exploring the combined, interactive effects on firm-labor dynamics remains limited. This study addresses this gap by examining how the interplay between firms and job candidates has changed since the advent of GenAI. Leveraging data from a leading bi-directional job matching platform in China, we investigate key pipeline metrics, from initial communication (measured by the volume of chats, resumes, and contact information exchanged) to final conversion (operationalized as the successful scheduling of an interview), across job categories differentially exposed to GenAI. Our findings demonstrate that positions highly exposed to AI experience a significant increase in overall communication volume, yet no corresponding change in interview conversions. Further analyses reveal that these observations stem from asymmetric shifts in communication and conversion patterns between firms and candidates. Specifically, among highly AI-exposed positions, candidates initiate significantly more communication but achieve fewer interview conversions, while firms initiate less communication yet secure more conversions. A dynamic regression analysis confirms the persistence of these divergent trends throughout our observation period. We provide strong mechanistic evidence for this pattern: GenAI devalues domain-specific knowledge while elevating skill transferability, thereby lowering entry barriers for ex-ante ineligible candidates and expanding the applicant pool with AI-augmented generalists. We discuss implications for both firms and individuals navigating this evolving job market landscape.

title: The Demands of Financial Education in the Face of the Markets' "Golden Calf": The Role of Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: University of Foggia

detail.title: The Demands of Financial Education in the Face of the Markets' "Golden Calf": The Role of Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: The growing pervasiveness of artificial intelligence in financial markets is exposing retail investors to unprecedented forms of cognitive and informational asymmetry, as recently underscored by ESMA's 2025 Warning on the use of AI-driven tools in investment decisions. The purpose of this article is to investigate the regulatory and dogmatic implications of this phenomenon at the intersection of the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), the MiFID framework, and the Italian Consolidated Law on Finance (TUF). The methodology adopted is dogmatic and comparative-regulatory: the notion of "AI system" is reconstructed as an organisational rather than a merely technological entity, and is then tested against the allocation of liability along the AI value chain (Article 25 AIA), the conceptual distinction between control and authority underpinning the deployer category, and the emerging paradigm of AIas-a-service in financial intermediation. Particular attention is devoted to fin-influencers and large diffusion models (LDMs) as new vectors of systemic risk, and to the IOSCO 2025 Report's recommendations on supervisory convergence. The article concludes that, where algorithmic opacity erodes the traditional pillars of investor protection, financial education must be reconceived as a constitutional precondition for the effective exercise of the economic freedoms; the principle of technological neutrality, far from being a passive regulatory stance, is reinterpreted as an active duty to safeguard the human dimension of financial choice-the actus humanus-against the seductive promises of algorithmic infallibility, which the article evokes through the metaphor of the markets' "golden calf".

title: NINE EMERGING STRUCTURAL PRESSURES SHAPING INSTITUTIONAL CONTINUITY: Institutional Reflections on Systemic Coordination, Infrastructure and Accountability Institute Working Paper Series Public Canonical Edition

detail.title: NINE EMERGING STRUCTURAL PRESSURES SHAPING INSTITUTIONAL CONTINUITY: Institutional Reflections on Systemic Coordination, Infrastructure and Accountability Institute Working Paper Series Public Canonical Edition
detail.abstract:
Institutions globally are increasingly operating within environments characterized by technological acceleration, infrastructure interdependence and systemic coordination complexity. Across finance, telecommunications, public administration, artificial intelligence, logistics, energy systems and digital infrastructure, continuity pressures may increasingly emerge not solely from isolated institutional disruption, but from interactions between rapidly evolving operational systems and slower-moving coordination structures.

This paper presents nine institutional reflections on emerging structural pressures shaping interconnected operational environments. Drawing upon historical precedent, infrastructure interdependence and recurring institutional dynamics observed across previous periods of technological and geopolitical transition, the paper examines how continuity, accountability and governance adaptation may evolve within increasingly accelerated systems.

Topics explored include artificial intelligence acceleration, semiconductor dependency concentration, supply-chain continuity, governance timing pressures, demographic transition, public-health coordination and strategic infrastructure resilience. Across these reflections, a recurring observation emerges: many institutional disruptions historically evolved not solely from informational absence, but from delayed coordination adaptation, fragmented continuity planning and governance evolution occurring after operational acceleration had already intensified.

Rather than presenting predictive certainty, the paper offers continuity-oriented institutional reflections intended to support broader strategic dialogue surrounding institutional resilience, coordination visibility and governance adaptation within interconnected operational environments.

The paper concludes by suggesting that institutional resilience within accelerated systems may increasingly depend on earlier coordination capacity, continuity visibility and adaptive accountability structures capable of evolving alongside increasingly interconnected technological and operational ecosystems.

title: A Comparative Study of CNN and Transfer Learning Models for Image-based AQI Prediction
affiliations: and Sinhgad Institute of Management, Pune

detail.title: A Comparative Study of CNN and Transfer Learning Models for Image-based AQI Prediction
detail.abstract: Air pollution is a significant environmental and public health concern, especially in countries such as India and Nepal. Conventional air quality monitoring relies on sensor-based systems, which are often costly and limited in coverage. This study proposes an image-based approach for predicting Air Quality Index (AQI) using deep learning techniques. A dataset of over 12,000 labelled images is used to train Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and transfer learning models. Preprocessing techniques such as resizing, normalization, and data augmentation are applied to improve model performance. The models learn visual patterns such as haze and reduced visibility associated with different pollution levels. Results indicate that deep learning methods can effectively classify extreme AQI categories, while moderate levels remain challenging due to similar visual features and environmental variations. The findings suggest that image-based AQI prediction can serve as a cost-effective and scalable alternative to traditional monitoring systems, with potential for further improvement through integration with additional environmental data.

title: When Trust Becomes Symbolic: Standards and the Governance of AI
affiliations: University of Glasgow

detail.title: When Trust Becomes Symbolic: Standards and the Governance of AI
detail.abstract:
Purpose-_This paper aims to reconceptualise standardisation as a generative governance arrangement that organises expectations, trust and decision-making under persistent uncertainty. Drawing on Niklas Luhmann's systems theory and extending Kim's (2025a) concept of standards as thematic identities and expectational structures, it seeks to explain how standards operate beyond technical coordination. Focusing on the UK's AI standards strategy, the paper examines how standards and strategy function as programmes at semantic and structural levels. In doing so, it explores how AI assurance practices are shaped and trust recast as an organisationally produced outcome rather than an inherent property of AI systems.

Design/methodology/approach-_The study adopts a qualitative, theory-driven analytical approach grounded in systems theory. It combines conceptual reconstruction with an in-depth case analysis of the UK AI standards and assurance ecosystem. Primary materials include UK policy documents, standards strategies, assurance roadmaps and regulatory guidance, complemented by secondary academic literature on standardisation and AI governance. These materials are analysed through Luhmannian concepts such as second-order observation, decision premises and programmes, enabling a semantic and structural analysis of how standards are institutionalised and operationalised within contemporary AI governance.

Findings-_The paper finds that AI standards in the UK operate as multi-layered observational procedures that institutionalise trust by stabilising expectations rather than guaranteeing technological reliability. Standards and strategy function as interlinked programmes: semantically, they construct thematic identities such as "trusted AI"; structurally, they embed decision premises across assurance practices. The analysis shows that standards oscillate between dissemination media and symbolically generalised communication media, enabling coordination through simplified symbols like certification. This oscillation produces ambivalent effects, simultaneously facilitating governance while fostering strategic ignorance and the ritualisation of AI ethics.

Originality/value-_This paper makes an original contribution by systematically linking Niklas Luhmann's core concepts-second-order observation, decision premises and programmes-to the standards and standardisation literature. Extending Kim's (2025a) concept of standards as thematic identities and expectational structures, it reconceptualises AI assurance as a multi-layered observational procedure in which trust is produced through recursive processes of decision and validation rather than embedded in AI systems. By theorising standards as mediating forms that oscillate between dissemination media and symbolically generalised communication media, the paper offers a novel Luhmannian explanation of how standards stabilise expectations while generating ambivalence, strategic ignorance and the ritualisation of ethics in contemporary AI governance.

title: A Scalable Framework for End-to-End Financial Data Reconciliation and Validation in Multi-Layer Reporting Systems

detail.title: A Scalable Framework for End-to-End Financial Data Reconciliation and Validation in Multi-Layer Reporting Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the research reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, animal subjects, or personal identifiable data. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently by the author. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract: Financial data reconciliation remains a critical challenge in multi-layer reporting systems, where records undergo complex semantic transformations across distributed architectures. Existing approaches rely either on manual validation or application-layer observability frameworks, which introduce memory and dependency bottlenecks that compromise deterministic auditability. This paper presents a practical formalization of a push-down reconciliation strategy that embeds deterministic validation directly within columnar storage layers using cryptographic hashing. The primary theoretical contribution is the formalization and complexity analysis of a distributed hash-based reconciliation algorithm that reduces traditional O(N log N) sorting bounds to O(N/p) execution time under massively parallel processing (MPP) constraints. We propose a decoupled, multilayer architecture establishing discrete validation checkpoints governed by a severity-aware exception classification model. Empirical evaluation on a reproducible 5-million-row synthetic financial dataset with controlled ground-truth discrepancy injection demonstrates the framework's correctness and efficiency. The push-down approach achieves 0.427 ± 0.009 seconds with perfect precision and recall (1.000/1.000) across all three discrepancy categories: mutated records, orphaned records, and ghost records. Compared against a naive application-layer pandas baseline (3.261±0.409 seconds), the proposed methodology yields a 7.6× reduction in execution time while eliminating cross-engine floating-point drift that produces false positives in applicationlayer tools. Attempts to benchmark against AWS Deequ and Great Expectations revealed critical runtime incompatibilities under current dependency stacks, underscoring a broader operational risk of application-layer validation frameworks in production financial systems. This framework transitions financial data reconciliation from a reactive auditing task into a continuous, deterministic control mechanism. All benchmark code and the dataset generator are publicly available.

title: Concept of Smart Citizens' Self-Library: A Conceptual and Applied Study in the Sri Lankan Context

detail.title: Concept of Smart Citizens' Self-Library: A Conceptual and Applied Study in the Sri Lankan Context
detail.abstract: Every person has a wide range of knowledge and resources. When this personal knowledge is properly structured and shared, it creates a "self-library", which is unique to the individual. If more people adopt this practice, the collective outcome becomes a significant repository of knowledge and resources, which is conceptualized in this comprehensive study as the self-library of smart citizens. With the advent of new technologies that facilitate information sharing, the modern citizen has digital access and rights, which empower them as "smart citizens" who can contribute and share with such a system and utilize their knowledge for production. This study presents the conceptual framework of the Smart Citizens Self-Library and explores its feasibility and implementation strategies. The main objective is to develop and organize people's procedural, experiential, and conceptual knowledge along with physical and digital resources in digitally indexable and shareable formats within the contemporary digital platforms that are accessible through public digital devices such as smartphones, computers, smartwatches, etc. This organized digital platform will serve as an information and resource distribution hub, enabling people to connect, disseminate, and access knowledge and resources efficiently. Using suitable software applications and digital platforms, users will be able to access the content based on their preferences, using famous delivery services that are affiliated with digital platforms (e.g., Uber, PickMe), conventional postal services, and courier services, and integrate income-generating tools through digital marketing strategies. Other enterprises can also be included as stakeholders to align with their commercial interests on seasonal promotions, and product advertisements can be incorporated as revenue-generating tools. The primary objective of this study was to determine optimal methods for indexing and classifying different types of knowledge and resources. Secondary objectives included identifying user groups interested in sharing and learning from such content and determining popular categories of shareable content.

title: Compute Substrate: A Permissionless Computation Layer Without Authority
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Compute Substrate: A Permissionless Computation Layer Without Authority
detail.abstract: We present Compute Substrate, a permissionless proof-of-work network for producing and persisting speculative computation without semantic, decision or outcome-level authority. Compute Substrate introduces a new class of infrastructure: a public cognition layer that is cryptographically persistent but structurally incapable of exercising power. Participants submit proposals (opaque computational outputs) and attestations (support signals) at a cost. The network aggregates these signals deterministically and commits them to a public ledger. Compute Substrate does not determine correctness, resolve outcomes, or trigger actions. Its sole purpose is to maintain a reproducible, cost-bearing history of what was proposed and supported over time, while remaining safe to ignore.

title: Kleo: Designing a European Digital Commons for Social Communication -Open Protocols, Digital Sovereignty and Value-Centred Architecture in the EU Normative Framework

detail.title: Kleo: Designing a European Digital Commons for Social Communication -Open Protocols, Digital Sovereignty and Value-Centred Architecture in the EU Normative Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This research was conducted independently, without any financial support from private entities. The author is an employee of a public administration body (Regione Emilia-Romagna, Italy) and has no personal or financial relationship with any of the platforms, organizations, or technologies discussed in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper involves no human subjects, clinical studies, or participant data collection.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
The dominance of a handful of non-European platforms over the digital communication landscape of the European Union constitutes one of the most consequential structural asymmetries of the contemporary information environment. Facebook, X, Instagram, TikTok and WhatsApp were designed around a single economic imperative-maximising user attention and behavioural data extractionwhose systemic effects include the amplification of disinformation, the erosion of mental health, the entrenchment of filter bubbles, and the near-total transfer of digital sovereignty from citizens and institutions to private operators subject to non-European jurisdiction.

This paper argues that the European Union possesses, for the first time, both the normative instruments and the technical preconditions to construct a credible alternative. The legislative corpus enacted between 2016 and 2024-comprising the GDPR, the NIS2 Directive, the Digital Markets Act, the Digital Services Act, the AI Act and the revised eIDAS 2.0 Regulation-establishes a coherent framework of rights, obligations and enforcement mechanisms that no major platform currently satisfies by design. The CLOUD Act exposure of US-hosted data, the mandatory interoperability obligations introduced by the DMA, and the institutional launch of the Digital Commons EDIC in December 2025 further define a geopolitical and structural context in which the construction of a European alternative has become not only desirable but strategically urgent.

We propose Kleo-a conceptual and architectural design for a European social communication ecosystem built on the Matrix open protocol, verified digital identity via eIDAS, and a value-driven information architecture that inverts the core assumptions of the attention economy. Kleo articulates four functionally distinct social spaces: private relational communication with hierarchical privacy, a certified public feed reserved for verified Trustcasters and an institutional channel integrating public administration and territorial health services. Each design choice-from a semantically structured reaction system replacing generic likes, to an explicit feed-completion mechanism (Catch-up Mode) designed to return time to the user rather than extract it, to a fully explainable recommendation algorithm compliant with the AI Act-is derived from the declared value postulate rather than retrofitted to regulatory requirements.

The feasibility of the proposed architecture is demonstrated through a working prototype that implements the core components of the ecosystem using an exclusively open-source and European technology stack. The paper concludes that the obstacles to a platform like Kleo are not technical but structural-governance, scale, institutional partnership and the relational lock-in of existing networks-and that the current normative and geopolitical moment provides an unprecedented conjunction of conditions under which those obstacles may, for the first time, be systematically addressed.

title: Reference Inversion and the Loss of Corrigibility

detail.title: Reference Inversion and the Loss of Corrigibility
detail.abstract: Adaptive systems rely on models to compress complexity, anticipate outcomes, and guide action. These models remain adaptive only while they remain corrigible: open to correction by the reality or substrate conditions they are designed to represent. This paper introduces reference inversion as a general failure mode in which a model displaces external reality as the effective reference signal. What begins as a cost-reducing consultant becomes a self-preserving commander. Negative feedback converts into positive feedback: error no longer updates the model, but is reinterpreted, suppressed, or displaced to protect model coherence. We develop a control-theoretic framework centered on a recurring cascade: reference inversion initiates the phase shift; compensatory amplification deepens the error; sub-threshold perturbation prevents early detection; habituation lock-in normalizes the distortion; reference clamping stabilizes the model; and performance-substrate divergence masks deterioration beneath apparent success. The framework is organized by the heuristic stability condition A w > D • L, where meta-referential awareness (A w) must exceed the product of mediation depth (D) and feedback latency (L) for corrigibility to persist. A central contribution is the late-feedback trap: corrective signals often arrive only after the system has habituated to distortion and the correction window has narrowed. Under such conditions, insight may reveal the error only after the time, energy, plasticity, trust, capital, or developmental openness required for low-cost repair has already been spent. If the model has already been transmitted to successors or offspring, delayed correction can become intergenerational reference transfer: the next system begins operating under the inherited map before the original system recognizes its failure. The framework situates reference inversion within cybernetics, predictive processing, self-model theory, narrative identity, interoception, allostatic load, Goodhart's law, organizational defensive routines, and artificial model collapse. RIF proposes a unifying failure topology in which representations become dangerous when they acquire authority without remaining accountable to the substrate they were built to serve. Reference inversion is offered not as a universal theory of suffering or failure, but as a recurring, diagnosable pattern in sufficiently complex, model-dependent adaptive systems.

title: Infrastructure Meets Intelligence: Governance Architecture, Not Digital Investment, as the Primary Determinant of Programme Trajectory -Evidence from 111 National Cases

detail.title: Infrastructure Meets Intelligence: Governance Architecture, Not Digital Investment, as the Primary Determinant of Programme Trajectory -Evidence from 111 National Cases
detail.abstract:
Digital investment does not explain governance success. Across 111 national cases, this paper demonstrates that the Action Research Maturity Index (ARMi) — a measure of structured participatory learning in programme governance architecture — is the primary determinant of long-run reform trajectory, independent of infrastructure spending.

The finding emerges from a striking contrast. Saudi Arabia and Denmark score 0.944 and 0.939 on the Digital Skills Maturity Index (DSMI) and are statistically indistinguishable by conventional rankings. Yet Saudi Arabia's ARMi is 0.572; Denmark's is 0.803. The gap is not in technology — it is in governance architecture. Band analysis across all 111 cases confirms this is not an outlier: mean ARMi is flat across low, mid, and high DSMI cohorts (0.645, 0.637, 0.662).

Three evidential threads substantiate the claim. The six highest ARMi scorers — Norway (0.860), Iceland and Sweden (0.825), Denmark (0.803), Rwanda (0.794), South Africa (0.791) — all achieved high ARMi through design-stage institutional separation of participatory governance from technology delivery, across three regions and two income categories. Three US Federal failures — Medicare (ARMi=0.528), the VA Electronic Health Record Modernisation ($49.8 billion, four veteran deaths), PECOS 2.0 ($200 million, zero output) — show that absence of this separation produces predictable failure at scale. Two China cases — BSN Blockchain and Ping An Finance-AI, both ARMi=0.62 — demonstrate that authority-concentrated architectures achieve world-scale deployment; their identical ARMi ceiling across radically different sectors points to a structural constraint on adaptive recalibration across political generations.

The US pattern is a governance equivalent of Porter's stuck-in-the-middle position: heavy infrastructure investment with neither Nordic participatory architecture nor Chinese operational focus.

The ARC (Adaptive Realist Construct) pipeline — the AMDG 111-case infrastructure integrated with the Maestro scenario protocol — provides a pre-programme structural diagnosis of governance failure risk that standard indices cannot supply. Four falsifiable propositions and a practitioner diagnostic framework are advanced. The manuscript is an SSRN Working Paper; appendices are offered as an online journal addendum.

title: The Ceremony of Having Decided: Human-in-the-Loop Oversight as Liability Architecture

detail.title: The Ceremony of Having Decided: Human-in-the-Loop Oversight as Liability Architecture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved review of publicly available documentation, peer-reviewed literature, and industry publications. No human subjects were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The author conducted this work independently without financial support from any organization.

detail.abstract: Human-in-the-loop (HITL) oversight is the consensus answer to AI governance, appearing in regulatory proposals, corporate frameworks, and public reassurances as the load-bearing safeguard against autonomous system harm. This paper argues that HITL functions primarily as liability architecture rather than a genuine safety mechanism, and that even a hypothetically perfected version would fail because the governed object is not the kind of thing authorization-based oversight can govern. I advance three claims. First, HITL as currently practiced operates as a ceremony of approval; reviewers facing time pressure, opaque system reasoning, and institutional incentives to approve produce documented automation bias (Mosier et al., 1998; Skitka et al., 1999; Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) rather than meaningful judgment. Second, the human judgment held up as the corrective baseline is itself inconsistent, context-dependent, and emotionally modulated; the appeal to human oversight as a stable reference point does not survive empirical scrutiny. Third, AI systems are non-deterministic objects whose behavior shifts with retraining, context, and deployment (Chen, Zaharia, & Zou, 2024); governance frameworks designed for deterministic objects (bridges, financial records, employees) cannot be adapted to govern something that does not hold still between observations. Recent "adaptive governance" proposals remain structurally bound to the same authorization paradigm they seek to replace, applying deterministic audit logic on shorter cycles. The paper does not propose a solution. It argues that correctly identifying the category of the problem is a prerequisite for finding one, and that the current institutional investment in HITL is not a partial answer but an active obstruction of better questions.

title: The Evidence-Safety Gap in Cryptographic Agent Governance: Compliance-Complete Failures and the Limits of Receipt-Based Accountability

detail.title: The Evidence-Safety Gap in Cryptographic Agent Governance: Compliance-Complete Failures and the Limits of Receipt-Based Accountability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of AEOESS and developer of the Agent Passport System (APS), the reference implementation cited in this paper. This self-reference is disclosed in Section 7.
declarations.funderStatement: No external research funding.

detail.abstract: Cryptographic agent governance systems use signed identities, delegated authority, policy decisions, and execution receipts to make autonomous AI agent actions auditable. These artifacts prove procedural validity. They do not, by themselves, prove that the action's effect is safe. This paper defines the Evidence-Safety Gap as an omitted-variable problem: the procedural validity predicate over identity, delegation, policy, action, and receipt excludes variables that may determine effect safety. We define compliance-complete failure as the simultaneous condition of procedural validity and unsafe effect. We characterize five omitted-variable classes: semantic state, population state, trust state, pipeline state, and temporal state. We motivate the framework through explicit defeat constructions against receipt-chain forensic signals and instantiate the failure class through constructive residual traces in an open-source reference implementation. The scenarios show construction, not prevalence. Two design implications follow: claim-scoped receipts and authorization-effect separation. Neither closes the gap. Both make it visible and auditable. The minimal contribution is the formal separation of procedural validity from effect safety in receipt-based agent accountability. The paper also gives a vocabulary for designing systems that do not let procedural validity silently become evidence of effect safety.

title: AI-Assisted ASC 606 Revenue Recognition for SaaS Businesses: Methodology, Validation Log, and Implications for SMEs

detail.title: AI-Assisted ASC 606 Revenue Recognition for SaaS Businesses: Methodology, Validation Log, and Implications for SMEs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no financial or personal relationships with other people or organizations that could inappropriately influence this work. This paper was produced independently with no external funding or sponsorship.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All work was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper documents the design, implementation, and iterative validation of a complete ASC 606 revenue recognition and SaaS metrics stack for a fictional software-as-a-service business, built using Python and AI-assisted development tools. The project produces a 10-tab Excel model, an interactive dashboard, and a 10-page disclosure package formatted as a 10-K financial statement footnote; output typically requiring a dedicated team over 8-12 weeks, completed by a single accounting professional in a fraction of that time. The paper makes four contributions: (1) a four-phase pipeline architecture with clean separation between data generation, recognition engine, metrics computation, and disclosure preparation; (2) a full validation log documenting seven material bugs found and fixed; (3) the accounting policy decisions, including modification treatment, material rights assessment, RPO exclusions, commission asset methodology, that required professional judgement and could not be delegated to the AI layer; and (4) a practical replication guide assessing what accounting knowledge, data infrastructure, and timeline an SME would realistically need to apply this approach. The central finding is that AI substantially lowers the execution barrier for complex financial reporting while leaving the governance barrier unchanged.

title: Data integration autonomy levels for Digital Twins in Industrial Automation: Classification and Prerequisites
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Data integration autonomy levels for Digital Twins in Industrial Automation: Classification and Prerequisites
detail.abstract: The increasing interconnectivity of industrial production systems has elevated the role of the Digital Twin (DT), which relies on high-fidelity data and its integration for process optimization and accurate state synchronization. As manufacturing environments become more dynamic and data-rich, traditional deterministic integration methods prove inflexible, while the proliferation of heterogeneous integration approaches has created a significant selection challenge for engineers.This paper presents a formalized framework for the systematic categorization and comparison of integration approaches to address this "paradox of choice". The methodology comprises a requirement classification to define varying industrial use cases and a capability taxonomy to evaluate the specific functionalities of integration solutions. A mapping methodology, supported by an automated mapping tool, facilitates the objective selection of the most suitable approach by penalizing technical underperformance and unnecessary architectural complexity.The framework was validated using a robotic assembly use case, demonstrating its utility in pinpointing technical fits and architectural deficiencies. Beyond providing decision support for practitioners, this research enables the academic community to objectively identify gaps in the research landscape, fostering the development of more efficient and scalable interconnected production systems.

title: The End of the Foundation Model Era: Commoditization, National Security, and the Path to AGI

detail.title: The End of the Foundation Model Era: Commoditization, National Security, and the Path to AGI

declarations.funderStatement: Independent research. No external funding.

detail.abstract: The foundation model era — roughly 2020 to 2025 — is over. The forces that defined it have inverted. Open source models have reached frontier performance while inference costs approach zero, exposing what was always structurally true: pre-training large language models at scale is not a durable competitive moat. The US government's formal designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk in February 2026 accelerated a transition already underway — but did not cause it. The paper argues that the AI industry is restructuring simultaneously along four axes: economic, as the circular financing structure that inflated foundation model valuations collapses; technical, as the pre-training scaling paradigm gives way to post-training optimization, test-time compute, and agentic composition; commercial, as application-layer integrators displace the foundation model companies whose commodity they now consume; and political, as the government asserts its historic role as gatekeeper of strategic technology. These are not separate disruptions. They are one structural shift, arriving together. The most consequential and least-discussed dimension is the permanent divergence between commercial AI and a classified national security AI track — built on different data, governed by different rules, and developing capabilities the public ecosystem cannot see, measure, or govern. Like every dual-use technology that has altered the calculus of state power, AI is being brought under government authority not by design but by the structural logic of what it is. The paper further argues that open-weight models are the counterintuitive instrument of sovereign control: a government that holds the weights commands the capability on its own terms, without dependence on vendor policy, financial continuity, or personnel clearance. The apparent openness of distributed model weights is, from a deploying government's sovereignty standpoint, the most governable architecture — because what cannot be withdrawn by a vendor's API policy cannot be taken away. The paper draws on public financial disclosures, primary government and corporate sources, and academic literature in AI scaling, innovation economics, and national security technology policy.

title: Financial Technology and Lending Practices in Nigeria: Access, Inclusion, and Consumer Trust in the Digital Credit Economy
affiliations: OpenFraudLabs

detail.title: Financial Technology and Lending Practices in Nigeria: Access, Inclusion, and Consumer Trust in the Digital Credit Economy
detail.abstract: This study examines how financial technology (fintech) is reshaping lending practices in Nigeria, particularly in relation to credit accessibility, financial inclusion, and consumer trust. In response to the limitations of traditional banking systems, fintech lending platforms have emerged as digital alternatives that offer faster loan processing, reduced documentation requirements, and broader access to underserved populations. Using a quantitative research approach, structured questionnaires were administered to 100 respondents with prior experience using digital lending platforms. The findings reveal that fintech lending significantly improves access to credit through speed, convenience, and minimal collateral requirements. However, major concerns remain regarding data privacy, unethical debt recovery practices, interest rate transparency, and consumer trust. While respondents generally viewed fintech platforms as more efficient and accessible than traditional banks, conventional financial institutions continued to perform better in areas such as trustworthiness, ethical perception, and long-term financial stability. The study concludes that fintech lending has strong potential to advance financial inclusion in Nigeria, but its long-term sustainability will depend on stronger regulation, responsible lending practices, improved data governance, and enhanced consumer protection frameworks.

title: Intelligent Testing Governance for Enterprise Systems: A Framework, Taxonomy, and Empirical Study of Intelligent Testing Failure Modes

detail.title: Intelligent Testing Governance for Enterprise Systems: A Framework, Taxonomy, and Empirical Study of Intelligent Testing Failure Modes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research was conducted independently and was not influenced by any personal or financial relationships with any organizations.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patient data, or animal subjects. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Enterprise software systems have grown beyond the reach of conventional testing approaches. At the scale at which modern retail, financial, and telecommunications platforms operate — processing millions of transactions daily across hundreds of interdependent services — testing is no longer a verification activity performed before release. It is a continuous, adaptive, intelligence-driven discipline embedded throughout the software lifecycle.

Yet despite the widespread adoption of AI-assisted testing tools, the governance of intelligent testing systems themselves remains largely unaddressed in the published literature. This paper addresses that gap.

We introduce the Intelligent Testing and Validation Framework for Enterprise-Scale Systems (ITESVF), a five-layer governance architecture that treats intelligent testing quality as a first-class operational property requiring its own observability infrastructure, failure taxonomy, and governance metrics.

We further introduce the Intelligent Testing Quality Index (ITQI), a composite metric for assessing intelligent testing system quality across five dimensions: signal collection, semantic validation, failure classification, adaptive orchestration, and continuous governance.

Preliminary observational findings from three enterprise deployments covering approximately 860 million transactions over 90-day observation periods suggest that ITQI scores of 32–44 may be typical of enterprise intelligent testing systems operating without dedicated governance infrastructure. Following ITESVF implementation, observed ITQI scores improved to 79–85, defect escape rates declined from 15–23% to 2–3%, and false coverage rates declined from 25–31% to 4–5%.

These are preliminary estimates based on practitioner-reported metrics and should be interpreted as indicative findings rather than definitive experimental results.

title: Towards high-capacity and low-distortion reversible database watermarking by improved histogram shifting and clustering
affiliations: Southwest University and Southwest University

detail.title: Towards high-capacity and low-distortion reversible database watermarking by improved histogram shifting and clustering
detail.abstract: In the big data era, databases as core information carriers face severe copyright disputes and illegal tampering during sharing and transactions. A reversible watermarking technique, characterized by the lossless recovery of the original data, enables copyright tracing while preserving data usability, thus becoming a critical solution. However, existing reversible database watermarking techniques generally struggle to balance distortion control and watermark capacity; most also rely on the primary key for grouping, making them vulnerable to invalidation via primary key erasure and incompatible with complex scenarios. To address these issues, a novel reversible database watermarking technique based on K-means clustering and improved histogram shifting (KCHSW) is proposed in this paper. Firstly, we adopt the K-means clustering algorithm to partition database tuples into as many groups as the watermark length. This not only aggregates more identical values into the same group to improve watermark capacity, but also eliminates the dependence on the primary key. Secondly, in each group, the error between the attribute value and its predicted value is calculated to generate a prediction error histogram. By traversing the frequency distribution of the histogram, the genetic algorithm is employed to select the optimal expansion interval in combination with the proposed capacity-distortion model. Experimental results verify the superiority of the proposed scheme, which effectively reduces data distortion while maximizing watermark capacity. Specifically, selecting optimal expansion intervals significantly mitigates the data distortion. Moreover, with more identical values by K-means, each group can embed more watermark bits, achieving a watermark capacity more than twice that of traditional histogram shifting methods.

title: From Autonomy to Initiative: Enterprise AI's Real Endgame
affiliations: Capgemini and  Capgemini

detail.title: From Autonomy to Initiative: Enterprise AI's Real Endgame
detail.abstract:
Current agentic AI discourse often treats autonomous execution as the apex of maturity — agents that operate independently within assigned parameters. We argue this is the wrong endpoint for enterprise AI in high-consequence environments. Autonomy is independence in how to work while remaining dependent on humans for what to work on. Initiative — the capacity to identify and prioritize action opportunities aligned with organisational purpose through immersion rather than instruction — is a categorically different capacity, and the one that determines whether enterprise AI generates value or merely generates output.

We define organizational intelligence as a system property: the capacity to perceive institutionally relevant patterns, infer their consequences, and select action opportunities under changing constraints. Governed knowledge is not intelligence itself — it is the substrate on which organizational intelligence operates. On this basis, we propose three conditions for governed initiative — initiative that is auditable, correctable, and institutionally legible: fertile pattern density above a perceptual threshold (Condition 1), a constraint-legible action space where governance rationale is causally transparent (Condition 2), and progressive governance relocation as the institutional world model deepens (Condition 3). We examine the professional consulting pyramid as a mature institutional analogue — one of several graduated immersion systems, including medical residency and military officer development, that satisfy all three conditions through accumulated exposure, legible constraints, and graduated relaxation of control as judgment develops.

For AI agents, each condition transforms in implementation but the functional requirements are identical. The central engineering claim is a three-step governance relocation mechanism: as the institutional world model deepens, governance enforcement migrates from explicit pre-action constraint checking (early lifecycle) through substrate-resident causal structure (mid lifecycle) to risk-based monitoring and audit sampling (mature lifecycle). We identify a substrate gap in the current literature — world models without governance and governance without world models each satisfy only a subset of the conditions — and propose six architectural enrichments to the Governed Intelligence Lifecycle (Paper D) that close it. We introduce the domain graph as the missing middle layer between the foundation model and application context: a governed, reusable, compounding substrate for domain-specific organizational intelligence.

Active inference (Friston, 2010) provides a normative model for describing why agents operating on deep, governed institutional world models may move from autonomous task execution toward institutionally legible initiative. We address the strongest counterargument — that scale alone may produce initiative without governed architecture — by scoping the claim: in regulated industries and enterprise deployments where agent actions carry material consequences, initiative must be auditable, correctable, and governable. Scale may produce initiative-like behaviour in low-consequence settings; governed architecture is necessary where initiative must be institutionally legible.

This is the capstone of a five-paper programme: Paper A (Reichhart and Gelas, 2026a) diagnoses dynamics blindness as the failure mechanism; Paper B (Gelas and Reichhart, 2026b) specifies the architectural resolution; Paper C (Reichhart and Gelas, 2026c) provides theoretical foundations from ten independent traditions; Paper D (Gelas and Reichhart, 2026d) operationalizes the governed intelligence lifecycle with epistemic immunity; this paper identifies the conditions under which that architecture produces governed initiative — agents that perceive what matters through immersion, not instruction.

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used publicly available secondary data and did not involve human participants or personal data requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Economic freedom as a. driver of ICT Service exports This paper examines whether economic freedom, as measured by the Index of Economic Freedom, has a positive and time-lagged impact on the share of ICT services exports in total service exports, and whether this effect corresponds to a regression coefficient of at least 0,20 per additional score point. The study is based on a dynamic panel data model according to Arellano-Bond using international secondary data, which maps time-delayed effects over up to ten years. The results show time-delayed effects: For lag 1 (ß = 0,827; p = 0,014) and lag 3 (ß = 0,418; p = 0,032), there is a positive and statistically significant influence that exceeds the required minimum coefficient. The remaining calculated lags are predominantly positive, but not statistically significant. The study thus confirms the hypothesis: an increase in economic freedom by one score point leads to a time-delayed increase in the share of ICT service exports. The result underscore the importance of open, constitutionally stable, and economically free framework conditions for the international competitiveness of digital service sectors and is therefore also relevant to economic policy.

title: Discovering the Why of Process Models – A Systematic Literature Review on Decision Mining
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Ottawa

detail.title: Discovering the Why of Process Models – A Systematic Literature Review on Decision Mining
detail.abstract: Within the field of Process Mining, process discovery is a data-driven method for discovering the control flow of processes—the how of a process. However, control flow alone does not explain why cases follow different branches at decision points. Decision Mining (DM) addresses this limitation by leveraging Machine Learning (ML) techniques to discover decisional criteria, also known as guards, from event logs. While two decades have passed since DM’s introduction, there is still no systematic and comprehensive overview of research in this field. This study presents a systematic literature review of DM, conducted across digital libraries using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, resulting in 30 primary research studies. We examine these articles from multiple perspectives, including investigated problems and proposed solutions, employed algorithms and available implementations, relevant application domains and datasets, and challenges that remain in the literature. Our findings identify four categories of DM research problems being investigated: problems related to event logs, types of decisions, evaluation practices, and model types. Across these categories, incomplete event logs—where key contextual data required to extract guards is missing—were the most prevalent problem. We further identified multiple challenges for the practical adoption of DM in process-aware information systems. The reviewed studies have mainly focused on decision trees, with limited uptake of more advanced ML algorithms or other types of techniques (e.g., local search) that may improve performance. We also found the literature fragmented, as studies rarely build upon earlier work or leverage advancements in the Process Mining field.

title: PHOENIX CENTER FOR ADVANCED LEGAL & ECONOMIC PUBLIC POLICY STUDIES
affiliations: Phoenix Center for Advanced Legal & Economic Public Policy Studies and University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: PHOENIX CENTER FOR ADVANCED LEGAL & ECONOMIC PUBLIC POLICY STUDIES
detail.abstract: This paper uses new data from the U.S. Census Bureau's Household Pulse Survey (Wave 2506) to examine demographic determinants of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and uses, fear of AI's career consequences, and active resistance to AI use. Regression analysis on a sample of 7,209 adults finds that AI use rises strongly with education and income and declines with age. In contrast, among those who have adopted AI, the breadth of use is driven primarily by education and age, with income playing little role beyond the adoption decision. Among users, concern about AI's impact on careers is concentrated among more educated and teleworking individuals, with income providing little explanatory power for career concern. Among non-users, sex and race are the dominant predictors of deliberate abstention. These findings have direct implications for AI literacy programs, workforce policy, and the design of consumer AI regulations.

title: Six Decades of Solutions: What Commercial Space Law Teaches AI Governance About Accountability
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Six Decades of Solutions: What Commercial Space Law Teaches AI Governance About Accountability
detail.abstract:
Frontier AI developers operate without mandatory liability, insurance, or enforceable

fiduciary duties — the private law mechanisms that discipline every other high-risk

industry. Current AI governance discourse focuses almost exclusively on ex ante

regulation and voluntary commitments, leaving the question of ex post accountability

structurally unresolved. This paper argues that the missing analytical framework for

designing AI accountability mechanisms already exists in commercial space law: the only

domain where private actors have deployed capabilities with global systemic risk potential

without clear territorial jurisdiction, with externalities affecting populations that had no

representation in governance negotiations.

title: Trend and Selection: A Behavioral Framework for Understanding Core Economic Principles -A Car Analogy Approach

detail.title: Trend and Selection: A Behavioral Framework for Understanding Core Economic Principles -A Car Analogy Approach
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel conceptual framework for understanding consumer behavior and macroeconomic fluctuations through the lens of two foundational psychological forces: Trend and Selection. Trend is defined as demand driven by social imitation and conspicuous consumption, while Selection represents demand driven by rational, need-based decisionmaking. Drawing on illustrative economic narratives and analogical reasoning rooted in Indian socioeconomic contexts, the paper argues that the interplay of these two forces constitutes the primary engine of economic movement, influencing interest rate differentiation, supply-demand volatility, price mechanisms, and monetary policy. The framework further introduces the concept of 'Daitya Mohini'-a structural influence dynamic categorically distinct from the contemporary social influencer-as the steering mechanism of economic cycles, and proposes that effective economic policy must manage the combined effect of Trend and Selection to maintain macroeconomic equilibrium. Policy implications are discussed across eight fundamental domains including pricing, monetary supply, investment regulation, taxation, wastage control, trade policy, and currency valuation. The paper presents a structural analysis demonstrating why citizen tax burdens of 2-10% of income are fiscally achievable under nationalized industry models, rising to 10-30% when industries are privatized and public revenue base is correspondingly reduced. Additionally, the paper Trend and Selection: A Behavioral Framework for Core Economics | Page 2 proposes a binding international principle prohibiting currency manipulation for political or competitive purposes, distinguishing permissible product price adjustments from impermissible currency value manipulation. The paper also presents a typology of economic agents (private versus social economists) and an original vehicle analogy for the structure of modern economies.

title: Drivers of Carbon Credit Adoption among Low-Cost Airline Passengers in Thailand: APLS-SEM Study of Consumer Attitudes, Perceived Value, and Behavioral Intention
affiliations: , Asia eLearning Management Center, Singapore, Iqra Business School - University Geomatika Malaysia, Iqra Business School - University Geomatika Malaysia and Mahasarakham Business School, Mahasarakham University, Thailand

detail.title: Drivers of Carbon Credit Adoption among Low-Cost Airline Passengers in Thailand: APLS-SEM Study of Consumer Attitudes, Perceived Value, and Behavioral Intention

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Review of Management and Marketing, volume 16, issue 4, 2026[10.32479/irmm.23298]

detail.abstract: This study investigates the key drivers of consumer adoption of carbon credits in the low-cost airline context in Thailand. Drawing on consumer behavior and sustainable marketing perspectives, the study examines how psychological, social, and economic factors shape passengers' attitudes, perceived value, and behavioral intention toward carbon offset programs. A quantitative survey of 500 low-cost airline passengers in Thailand was conducted. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was employed to test the proposed model linking environmental awareness, climate change concern, perceived environmental responsibility, trust in carbon credit programs, perceived effectiveness, social norms, and price sensitivity to attitude, perceived value, and behavioral intention. The findings indicate that environmental awareness, climate change concern, perceived environmental responsibility, trust in carbon credit programs, perceived effectiveness, and social norms positively influence consumer attitudes toward carbon credit adoption, while price sensitivity negatively affects attitude formation. Attitude significantly enhances perceived value, and both attitude and perceived value strongly predict consumers' intention to adopt carbon credits when purchasing low-cost airline tickets. This study relies on cross-sectional selfreported data from low-cost airline passengers in Thailand, which may limit causal inference and generalizability to other airline segments or national contexts. The results provide actionable insights for airline managers and marketers. Airlines should integrate carbon offset options into the ticketing process, enhance transparency and trust in carbon credit programs, communicate tangible environmental impacts, and design affordable pricing or bundled offers to increase perceived value among price-sensitive consumers.

title: A Study on Digital Nomadism and Cognitive-Affective Responses: Impact of Novel Environments on Remote Work Behaviour
affiliations: NSB Academy, Bengaluru, NSB Academy, Bengaluru, NSB Academy, Bengaluru and NSB Academy, Bengaluru

detail.title: A Study on Digital Nomadism and Cognitive-Affective Responses: Impact of Novel Environments on Remote Work Behaviour
detail.abstract: In today's remote work world, digital nomadism is a big trend. People mix work with travel. This study looks at how new places change remote workers' behavior through feelings and thoughts. We use the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-OR) model to see how fresh environments spark emotions and brain load, affecting productivity and interest in work. Methodology: We used a simple quantitative design with secondary data from Kaggle on remote work productivity and worker tiredness. We checked things like stress, fatigue, job happiness, and output using basic stats and correlations. Findings: New spots can excite workers and boost happiness, but they also tire the brain, mixing up productivity. Workers feel more engaged, yet too much strain hurts performance.

title: The Signal is the Ceiling: Measurement Limits of LLM-Predicted Experience Ratings from Open-Ended Survey Text
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: The Signal is the Ceiling: Measurement Limits of LLM-Predicted Experience Ratings from Open-Ended Survey Text

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors are employees of Dimension Labs, a causal intelligence platform that links unstructured customer conversations to business metrics, producing statistical evidence of what drives outcomes. The annotation described in this study was conducted on the Dimension Labs platform, which also provided the computational infrastructure used to execute the annotation pipeline. No external funding was received for this research. The study design, analysis, and interpretation were conducted independently by the authors.

detail.abstract: An earlier paper (Hong, Potteiger, and Zapata 'LLM Predictive Scoring and Validation' 2026) established that an unoptimized GPT 4.1 prompt predicts fan-reported experience ratings within one point 67% of the time from open-ended survey text. This paper tests the relative impact of prompt design and model selection on that performance. We compared four configurations on approximately 10,000 post-game surveys from five MLB teams: the original baseline prompt and a moderately customized version, crossed with three GPT models (4.1, 4.1-mini, 5.2). Prompt customization added roughly two percentage points of within-±1 agreement on GPT 4.1 (from 67% to 69%). Both model swaps from that best configuration degraded performance: GPT 5.2 returned to the baseline, and GPT 4.1-mini fell six percentage points below it. Both levers combined were dwarfed by the input itself: across capable configurations, accuracy varied more than an order of magnitude more by the linguistic character of the text than by the choice of prompt or model. The ceiling has two parts. One is a bias in how the model reads text, which prompt design can correct. The other is a difference between what fans write about and what they actually decide, which no engineering can close because the missing information is not in the text. Prompt customization moved the first part; model selection moved neither reliably. The result is not that "prompt engineering helps a little" but that prompt engineering helps in a specific and predictable way, on the part of the ceiling it can reach.

title: Breaking the Early Bell: Lessons from the First Statewide Mandate on School Start Times
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh, University of Pittsburgh, University of Pittsburgh and University of Edinburgh

detail.title: Breaking the Early Bell: Lessons from the First Statewide Mandate on School Start Times
detail.abstract:
We examine the impact of California’s Senate Bill 328 (SB 328), the first statewide mandate requiring later school start times for middle and high schools, on adolescent sleep, mental health, and academic outcomes. Using difference-in-differences and eventstudy designs across five data sources, we find that SB 328 increased the share of students sleeping at least 8 hours per night by 13%, meeting the CDC-recommended minimum for this age group. Average mental health effects are imprecisely estimated, but boys show significant reductions in sadness, hopelessness, and suicidal ideation, and Hispanic students, who experienced the largest sleep-timing shifts, show parallel reductions in difficulty concentrating; together these patterns are consistent with a dose-response relationship between sleep improvement and mental well-being. Math and English scores in grade 8 improved by approximately 0.08–0.10 standard deviations, with the largest gains among Hispanic and economically disadvantaged students. A within-state analysis using teachers’ commute arrival times as a proxy for pre-policy school start times corroborates these findings, and shows academic gains accumulating over 2023–2025 alongside a suggestive decline in high school dropout rates. The absence of effects on chronic absenteeism rules out an attendance-driven mechanism, pointing instead to the direct cognitive benefits of aligning school schedules with adolescents’ biological rhythms.

title: Anti-Harassment Policy and the Startup Labor Market
affiliations: University of Illinois at Chicago,  and Southern Methodist University (SMU) - Finance Department

detail.title: Anti-Harassment Policy and the Startup Labor Market
detail.abstract:
This paper examines how anti-harassment legal reforms that weaken non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) in cases of workplace sexual harassment affect startups' hiring and organizational decisions. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design and LinkedIn data on over 50,000 U.S. venture-capital-backed startups from 2014–2022, we find that NDA reforms, although intended for employee protection, reduce female hiring by about 8%, with effects concentrated among junior women, who are statistically more prone to sexual harassment, and in small or male-dominated startups. The results apply to both the intensive and extensive margins of female hiring. Treated entrepreneurial firms also witness more departures of male managers, promote more women, and receive less VC funding. These results suggest that while NDA-weakening laws increase firms’ perceived legal risk and reduce female hiring, they also trigger internal restructuring that promotes women's advancement into leadership and may, over time, foster more accountable and inclusive organizational cultures.

title: The Pause That Wasn't Hesitation: Validating What Platform Traces Really Mean
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Management

detail.title: The Pause That Wasn't Hesitation: Validating What Platform Traces Really Mean
detail.abstract: Platform traces are abundant, psychologically tempting, and increasingly consequential when embedded in automated interventions. We develop an evidence-to-permission mapping for platform behavioral metadata: before a trace is labeled as a user state or used for treatment, researchers should assign it to the population, construct domain, and use class its evidence warrants. We apply the mapping to three timestamp traces from a leading Chinese ticketing platform. Among 108,924 completed transactions, pre-payment hesitation time (PPHT) initially looks like hesitation, but stronger tests reassign it to account-keyed latency: PPHT-only prediction is near chance, residual PPHT does not predict no-show, account structure explains 72.1% of PPHT variance, and repeated accounts are stable (ICC = 0.464). By contrast, advance-purchase timing behaves as an event-structured planning trace whose no-show association survives saturated fixed effects, while check-in timing is an attendee-arrival operations trace observed only after attendance. The completed-transaction scope is essential: PPHT may still capture hesitation at the unobserved abandonment margin. The paper shows that platform-log validity is not a trace-construct property alone, but a trace-construct-population-use relation governing what researchers and platforms may infer, report, and automate.

title: AlphaGlass: Interpretable Characteristic-Based Portfolio Choice
affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology - Department of Economics and Management, University of California, Berkeley, University of California - Haas School of Business and Karlsruhe Institute of Technology - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: AlphaGlass: Interpretable Characteristic-Based Portfolio Choice
detail.abstract:
We propose AlphaGlass, an inherently interpretable machine-learning framework for constructing portfolios that directly optimize investment objectives. AlphaGlass maps stock characteristics into additive signals with sparse interactions and converts these signals into long-short portfolios through a differentiable rank-and-mask layer. This end-to-end design allows the model to optimize objectives such as the Sharpe ratio or mean-variance utility while keeping portfolio weights interpretable and traceable to specific characteristics and interactions. We show theoretically that in-sample objective maximization consistently estimates the population objective and that the differentiable rank-and-mask layer is a faithful smooth proxy for the corresponding conventional long-short quantile portfolio. In U.S. equities, AlphaGlass delivers strong out-of-sample performance and reveals economically interpretable drivers of long and short positions.

title: Algorithmic Credentialism
affiliations: Harvard University - Harvard Graduate School of Education and Harvard University

detail.title: Algorithmic Credentialism
detail.abstract:
The paper develops a framework for evaluating credential-coded algorithmic screens under existing civil rights law. AI-powered hiring tools trained on historical data often encode and automate bachelor's degree requirements as a proxy for worker skill, producing what this paper terms algorithmic credentialism. Drawing on labor economics research on workers Skilled Through Alternative Routes (STARs), disability theory's critique of the medical model, and disparate-impact doctrine from Griggs v. Duke Power Co. through the Civil Rights Act of 1991, it argues that such screens misidentify the source of hiring exclusion, locating it in the worker rather than in the design of the selection system. This institutional-design problem is amenable to evaluation under the existing disparate-impact doctrine. Under the paper's proposed framework, a credential-coded screen producing disparate impact triggers a legal obligation to validate the screen as job-related and consistent with business necessity, with skills-based hiring supplying the less-discriminatory alternative. The paper further argues that the efficiency rationale historically offered for degree screens is weakened, not strengthened, by AI. The same computational power that automates credentialism at scale can instead match applicants to jobs on multidimensional skill profiles, making the bachelor's degree a less necessary (and less legally defensible) proxy than it was in the pre-AI labor market.

title: Deep Research on a Loop: Using AI Agents to Construct Economic Datasets
affiliations: University of Buenos Aires (UBA) - Faculty of Economic Science, Students, Department of Economics,  and University of San Andres (UdeSA)

detail.title: Deep Research on a Loop: Using AI Agents to Construct Economic Datasets
detail.abstract:
Constructing datasets from primary sources is one of the costliest tasks in empirical economics. We propose Deep Research on a Loop (DRIL), a methodology that uses AI agents to assemble datasets from publicly available sources. DRIL applies a fixed research instrument across a mapped unit space (e.g., countries by years), with a two-stage architecture separating design from implementation. The instrument specifies variables and coding rules, an evidence policy governs sources and citations, and data quality mechanisms track gaps and uncertainty explicitly. We exercise DRIL on a 2025 update of the Global Tax Expenditures Database for eight Latin American and Caribbean countries. The run produces 129 sources and 136 evidence records, covering 22 qualitative fields fully and 6 quantitative estimate types with documented gaps, at the cost of a standard LLM subscription comparable to a few hours of research-assistant work. We argue that even partial automation of dataset construction can shift the production function of empirical economics.

title: Mortality Rates by Race and Ethnicity Among People with Disabilities
affiliations: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), University of California, Berkeley and Hunter College, CUNY

detail.title: Mortality Rates by Race and Ethnicity Among People with Disabilities
detail.abstract:
This paper uses Medicaid claims data from 2017-2021 to measure racial/ethnic disparities in mid-life mortality among low-income adults with disabilities receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI). We find that American Indian and Alaska Native and White SSI recipients have the highest age-adjusted mid-life mortality rates (2.9% and 2.6%, respectively), followed by Black and Hispanic recipients (2.3% and 1.9%), and then Asian recipients (1.6%). We also find differences in diagnosed chronic conditions, "despair-related" conditions, substance use disorders, and disabling conditions by race/ethnicity. Controlling for these differences attenuates the White-Hispanic, White-Asian, and AIAN-White mortality gaps; however, differences in clinical diagnoses by race do not affect the White-Black mortality gap. Our results show that within a socioeconomically vulnerable population, Black adults outlive Whites.
